# **Shepherd's Eye**
**CN:** 0 **Range:** Special **Target:** Special **Duration:** Instant

This spell is most often used to find lost livestock, but is easily put to other uses. You grab a bit of organic matter belonging to a single creature — wool, blood, a piece of their leavings — and add it to a bowl of water. After scrying into the bowl for 10 - IB minutes, secret symbols appear to your sight: the GM will describe the creature's location. If you are familiar with the location, you know where they are.
# **Lore of Witchcraft**

Ingredients for Witchcraft only reduce Miscast level if you roll 01–40 on a Miscast table (keep the roll if moving down to a new table). They are, however, cheap and readily available: herbs and body parts of small animals for the most part. Ingredients cost a Spell's CN in brass pennies to purchase. Alternatively, you may spend 2 hours foraging with an **Average (+2 SL) Lore (Herbs)**, **Outdoor Survival**, or **Set Trap** Test: a success produces 1 + SL ingredients. The Lore of Witchcraft may be used with Channelling (*Dhar*) or Channelling (Magick).

**Ingredients:** Witches use a medley of common herbs and a horrific mixture of animal body parts, often harvested when a creature is still alive. It is not uncommon to find them clutching lizard eyes, dog toes, donkey gizzard, or much, much worse in their bloody hands as they cast their foul magics.
# **Blight**
**CN:** 14 **Range:** Willpower Bonus yards
**Target:** Special **Duration:** Instant
You cause an area to become blighted or desolate. For example you may target either a tavern, well, field, or a domestic animal. If you successfully cast the Spell, the target suffers from a blight:
- All food and drink in a blighted tavern immediately spoils.
- A blighted well becomes instantly brackish and stagnant.
- Any crops currently planted in a blighted field rot overnight.
- A blighted animal sickens. The afflicted beast no longer produces anything (cows produce no milk, coats and hides grow mangy and unusable) and will die in 10 - SL days.
# **Creeping Menace**
**CN:** 6 **Range:** Willpower yards
**Target:** 1 **Duration:** Willpower Bonus Rounds

You summon a swarm of creeping, slithering creatures to harass your foes. Each target affected is immediately Engaged by a swarm of Giant Rats, Giant Spiders, or Snakes (your choice of one creature type). Use the standard profiles for the relevant creature type, adding the *Swarm* Trait. For your Action, you may make a **Challenging (+0 SL) Charm Animal** Test to direct one or more swarms to attack a different target. When the Spell ends, any remaining swarms disappear into the shadows.

**CN:** 10 **Range:** Willpower yards
**Target:** 1 **Duration:** Willpower Bonus Rounds

- **Limb** Limb becomes useless, as if amputated (see page 177).
*Fatigued* and *Stunned* last for the duration. You may stab the doll again to affect an additional, unaffected Location by using an Action to take an **Average (+2 SL) Channelling** Test.

**Range:** Willpower yards *or* Willpower

md: # **CHARACTER SHEET EXPLAINED**

This sheet is where you keep track of your Character's abilities, equipment and more. Characteristics and Skills are often used to find out how well you perform an action. You will roll the dice (the two ten-sided dice known as D100, see page 6) and if the result is equal to or lower than the relevant Skill, your action succeeds. **The higher the value of your Skill, the easier it is to succeed**.
Other factors such as the difficulty of the task impact this too (see page 130) but for now it's enough to know that your Skill number is the basic chance of succeeding at a Challenging task.
**Prioritise the Skills you want your Character to be best at by placing the highest values and most Advances in those Skills and their associated Characteristics.**
- **Personal Details:** Name, Species (page 23), Appearance
- **Experience:** Your Gamemaster will award Experience Points, also called XP, ) you use to improve your Character's abilities (see page 191. Keep a record of your unspent, spent, and total XP.
- **Movement:** how quickly you can move (see page 40).
- **Fate and Fortune:** Help you succeed and survive (see page 133).
**Class and Career:** Your occupation (see page 36). Status (Brass/Silver/Gold) and Standing (your rank within your Status, the higher the better) show your wealth and position (page 140).

The Career Advancement Tracker tracks your progress through your Career. Each time you Advance a Skill or Characteristic, purchase a Talent, or gain a Trapping from a higher Career Level, tick a box. Once all the boxes before a numbered skull are ticked, you can increase your Career Level (page 43).

**Characteristics:** Your innate abilities, and the starting score for your Skills. The first digit (the 'tens' value) is your **Characteristic Bonus**, used in many rules. For example, your **Strength Bonus (SB)** is added to the damage you deal with melee attacks. Strength **37** gives an **SB of 3**, while **42** gives an **SB of 4**.
- **Weapon Skill:** aptitude for fighting hand-to-hand, with or without a weapon.
- **Ballistic Skill:** effectiveness with ranged weapons like bows and throwing knives.
- **Strength:** damage caused in fights, lifting weights, swimming and climbing.
- **Toughness:** physical hardiness, resisting damage, surviving harsh conditions and poisons.
- **Initiative:** thought/reaction speed, especially in battle or under pressure.
- **Agility:** coordination and athleticism, used in running, riding, leaping, or dodging.
- **Dexterity:** performing delicate manual tasks like playing a musical instrument or skilled manufacturing.
- **Intelligence:** powers of thought, analysis, and understanding. Useful for healing, evaluating, and general knowledge.
- **Willpower:** strength of mind, determination and focus.
- **Fellowship:** making a good impression and getting on with people.

Skills: learned and developed abilities. A Skill starts at the value
of its associated Characteristic (shown on the Character Sheet and/
or the entry for the relevant Skill in Chapter 4, page 110). Each
Advance increases it by +5. Your starting Skills come from your
Species and Career.
There are three types of Skill:
Basic Skills can be used by anyone, even without any Advances.
Advanced Skills can only be used if you have
at least one Advance in the Skill.
Grouped Skills cover broad areas. When you take an Advance,
choose a specialization such as Lore (Empire) or Lore (Tilea).
Armour: record your Armour (page 307) here, and write
the total Armour Points (APs) in the Armour diagram on the
front of the sheet.
Corruption and Mutation: exposure to Chaos leads to
Corruption and Mutation (page 187), but your Character
begins the game without such curses.
Trappings,
Encumbrance, and Wealth: the
equipment, clothes, weapons, and other items you carry. You
gain starting Trappings from your Class and Career, and
can buy or find more during play (see page 297). Record
each item’s Encumbrance and make sure you can carry it all
(see page 299). Wealth is measured in brass pennies, silver
shillings, and gold crowns.
Spells and Prayers: magical or religious Careers give
access to Spells (see page 240) or Prayers (see page 220).
Talents: special abilities, tricks and techniques with
individual game impacts (see page 114).
Ambition: your Character’s goals and dreams (see page 41).
Party Ambition is what keeps your party together — the goal
or agenda you share in common.
Wounds: how much damage you can take before
suffering Critical Injuries. Your starting maximum Wounds
are calculated from your Strength Bonus, Toughness Bonus
(doubled), Willpower Bonus, and any other modifiers, such as
the Hardy Talent (see page 40).
Damage reduces your Wounds, while Healing restores
them, up to your maximum (see page 170). Increasing your
Characteristics or gaining certain Talents can increase your
maximum Wounds. If you take Damage when you have 0
Wounds, you suffer a Critical Injury (see page 171). Record
any Critical Injuries and their effects in the large box.
Armour: Write the total Armour Points (APs) in each
location on the diagram. Armour Points reduce the damage
you take from weapons.

# **DWARFS**

Dwarfs are tough, resourceful, proud, and honourable. Given their long memories and proud natures, they bear grudges against those who have dishonoured them, even taking on the grievances of their ancestors. They believe their forebears watch over them, nursing bitterness long after death. Whilst it might be hard to win a dwarf 's friendship, once given, it is sincere and lasting.

They are squat and powerfully built, with thick hair and heavy features. The length of a dwarf 's beard is a mark of pride and status, and to shave it is a terrible shame. While not as ageless as the near-immortal elves, dwarfs can live for many centuries. Indeed, some say that as long as a dwarf has a purpose, they will not die unless struck down in battle.

Dwarfs are encountered throughout the Old World, although most reside in their holds, vast fortified mines dug deep beneath the mountains. For all their prowess in battle and expertise in craftsmanship, their civilisation is a shadow of its former glory and continues to decline. They often speak their own language, khazalid, but are reluctant to teach it to others. They use the name Karaz Ankor — meaning Everlasting Realm — to refer both to their ancient mountain empire and to the beleaguered holds that remain under dwarf control. The dwarf calendar begins in the year –4523 IC, when the Great Hall of Karaz-a-Karak was first established, and dwarfs still pay respect to the high king who sits upon its throne, though for those living in the Empire, he is a distant presence.
# **Opinions**
#### **On Reiklander Humans…**

*'Like my father's father's father's father, I've lived in the Reikland all my life. As folk go, they know not to mess with my business and show me the respect I deserve, as is right. Yes, they're unreliable, and as changeable as the wind, but they're also resourceful and shrewd, so I'd recommend them as business partners, as they see solutions I'd not even consider.'*
— Garral Herraksson, Jeweller from Eilhart
#### **On Halflings…**

*'I've heard they make sharp archers and nimble scouts, and that their culinary art makes folk grateful for their company. Well, a slice of chuff and a pint of ale keep me happy, and the halflings are too immature and vulnerable to adapt to life beyond their farms and pie shops.'*
— Bardin Hargirson, Mercenary from Karak Azgaraz
#### **On High Elves…**

*'Those lackbeards once raised their towers where Marienburg and Altdorf now stand before their great betrayal of our ancestors, the atrocities that led to the War of Vengeance. Well, we showed them, so now you barely see them hereabouts. Grudges may have been settled, but still, don't trust them.'*
— Dern Ketilsson, Diplomat from Karak Azgaraz
#### **On Wood Elves…**

*'On the far side of the mountains lies a benighted forest where no sensible folk travel. The trees there remember the bite of axes and are vindictive in their punishment of those who bear them. These wood spirits keep a clan of elves in their thrall, and many a dwarf of the Grey Mountains has suffered the sting of their arrows.'*

begins in the year –4523 IC, when the Great Hall of Karaz-a-
Karak was first established, and dwarfs still pay respect to the
high king who sits upon its throne, though for those living in
the Empire, he is a distant presence.
opinions
On Reiklander Humans…
‘Like my father’s father’s father’s father, I’ve lived in the Reikland all my
life. As folk go, they know not to mess with my business and show me
the respect I deserve, as is right. Yes, they’re unreliable, and as changeable
as the wind, but they’re also resourceful and shrewd, so I’d recommend
them as business partners, as they see solutions I’d not even consider.’
— Garral herraksson, Jeweller from eilhart
On Halflings…
‘I’ve heard they make sharp archers and nimble scouts, and that their
culinary art makes folk grateful for their company. Well, a slice of chuff
and a pint of ale keep me happy, and the halflings are too immature and
vulnerable to adapt to life beyond their farms and pie shops.’
— Bardin hargirson, Mercenary from Karak Azgaraz
On High Elves…
‘Those lackbeards once raised their towers where Marienburg and Altdorf
now stand before their great betrayal of our ancestors, the atrocities that
led to the War of Vengeance. Well, we showed them, so now you barely
see them hereabouts. Grudges may have been settled, but still, don’t
trust them.’
— Dern Ketilsson, Diplomat from Karak Azgaraz
On Wood Elves…
‘On the far side of the mountains lies a benighted forest where no sensible
folk travel. The trees there remember the bite of axes and are vindictive
in their punishment of those who bear them. These wood spirits keep a
clan of elves in their thrall, and many a dwarf of the Grey Mountains has
suffered the sting of their arrows.’
— rungni Garilsson, Scholar from Karak norn
Options: Animosity (Elves)
Given the long memories of dwarfs and their tendency to bear
grudges, many harbour a deep resentment towards elves for
their part in the War of Vengeance. As such, many dwarfs have
the Animosity (Elves) Psychology trait (see page 183 and 356).
Given some WFRP parties contain both elves and dwarfs, this
may lead to unhelpful tensions. So, you may prefer to ignore this
Talent between party members.

md: # **NOSING AROUND**

The Empire is rife with secretive schemes and dark conspiracies. Nobles expend a hundred lives to move a border two fields over, while the servants of the Dark Gods work to undermine civilisation itself.

Characters will inevitably find themselves uncovering these plots — examining the site of a grisly murder, poring over dusty records, following whispered rumours, and prising secrets from those who would rather keep silent.
#### **HIDING CLUES**
Don't hide vital clues behind a Test. It can be tempting to make Players work for information, but if finding that information is essential to the adventure, they should find it.

Instead, allow Characters to notice one or two important clues straight away. Use Perception or Intuition Tests to reveal additional clues, useful insights, or a clearer understanding of what has already been discovered.

Let the Players piece the evidence together where possible, and if they still become stuck, provide another lead. If all else fails, a helpful NPC can always point the way. An unsolved mystery is intriguing — one the Characters never discover is simply frustrating.
#### **COMMON MEANS OF INVESTIGATION AND RESEARCH**
| Action | Test |
| Tell how an animal died | An Average (+2 SL) Animal Care Test, or Challenging (+0 SL) if a subtle poison or illness was the cause. |
| Tell a lie, or spot one | The liar makes a Charm Test, opposed by the target's Intuition. The Difficulty can increase if the lie is particularly outrageous. |

| Ask around about someone | A Gossip Test to learn what others think of the subject, with better rolls revealing more secretive or pertinent information. A successful Bribery Test can tell you someone is corrupt enough to take a bribe, and what their price might be. |

| Wring a secret from someone | A Charm Test, opposed by the target's Cool to trick them into letting something slip, or an Intimidate Test opposed by Cool to force the information from them. The Difficulty is set by just how sensitive the information is. |
| Search a room or a crime scene | A successful Perception Test spots hidden or subtle details, with better results revealing more information. A disturbed scene increases the Test's Difficulty. |

| Extract information from books | A successful Research Test will tell you what library or book to consult to learn something, or help you find pertinent facts buried within large and mouldering tomes. |
| Recall a useful fact | Having an Advance in a Lore Skill will tell you basic information about that subject, with a Test required only to recall particularly obscure or unusual information. |
| Spot a forgery | An Evaluate Test, with a Difficulty set by the quality of the work. |
| Follow someone's trail | A Track Test, with a Difficulty set by the conditions and age of the trail. Opposed by your quarry's Track only if they took the time to cover their trail. |

# **5. TALENTS, TRAPPINGS, AND FINAL GAME DETAILS**
Talents are your special abilities, tricks, and techniques with individual game impacts (see page 114). **Choose a Talent from the first level of your Career and add it to your Character Sheet.**
Trappings are your equipment, clothes, weapons, and other carried items.
- All Characters begin with Clothing, a Dagger, and a Pouch.
- You also begin play with all of the Trappings from your Career's first level.
- Finally, you start with some Trappings common to your Class, as shown in the Class Trappings table.
You begin the game with an amount of coins decided by your Status:
### **STARTING WEALTH**
| Status Tier | Wealth |
| Brass | 20 brass pennies plus 2d10 per Standing Level |
| Silver | 10 silver shillings plus 1d10 per Standing Level |
| Gold | 2 gold crowns plus 1 per Standing Level |
Record each of these items on your Character Sheet. If you end up with two of something, keep the spare! You can always sell it if you wish, and a spare weapon can often come in handy.
So, if you were Brass 3, you would start with 6d10+20 Brass pennies; if Silver 3, you would begin with 3d10+10 silver shillings, and if you were Gold 3, you would have 5 gold crowns.
Money can be used to purchase more Trappings or saved for spending during play. Commonly available items and the relative worth of different coins are covered in **Chapter 11: Consumer Guide**.
# **Wounds**

md: *You had a quiet life before, I'd wager, mucking out a pigsty or kneeling at the feet of nobles for scraps. What fancy carried you thence? Adventure? Gold? Justice? Hah! You might as well confess to madness and be done.*

*Adventure is what fools call the miseries they've endured. Justice is a lie, though blood can be had in its place, if you've the stomach for it. Gold, on the other hand… that I can promise, provided you've the grit to earn it, and the wit not to ask too many questions…'*

These are the darkest of years, an era that prophets name the End Times. Karaz Ankor, the ancient empire of the dwarfs, is all but overrun. The elves have withdrawn to distant lands or cavernous forests. The Empire stands, but its foes muster in ever greater numbers, and nefarious cults plot and scheme within its borders. The Emperor Karl Franz, anointed to his position in 2502 IC by the will of the elector counts and the blessings of mighty Sigmar, rules with strength and wisdom that some nevertheless deem insufficient to the task.

Welcome to **Warhammer Fantasy Roleplay**, a game like no other. Here you will explore a world of glittering wonders, vile darkness, and everything in between. You will encounter feared and respected wizards who master their arts in the high towers of the Colleges of Magic, as well as witches who dabble in magics they barely understand. Priests, virtuous and fanatical in uneven measure, preach the word of the gods and caution against dark powers they fear to name. Proud ranks of soldiers march out to cheers and wage war on orcs, beastmen, and other invaders. They return scarred and diminished, or do not return at all.

Our protagonists are no heroes, assured of victory, gold, and glory. What they would gain, they must win, often against the odds, by strength, wit, and fortune. Coin is hard-earned and quickly spent, and the most lucrative opportunities pit would-be adventurers against hidden cults, bloodthirsty mercenaries, or inhuman beasts that dwell in dark forests or deep beneath the earth. Magic provides a powerful advantage, but it bears risks of its own, and there is no pyre so well fed that a witch hunter could not fit one more cur atop it. The gods heed the prayers of their most faithful, but they are jealous and fickle, quick to withdraw their blessing from those they no longer consider worthy.

This book contains everything you need, aside from a few dice and some paper and pencils. So gather your friends, appoint a gamemaster, and prepare to explore the grim and perilous world of **Warhammer Fantasy Roleplay**.
### **NEW TO ROLEPLAYING GAMES**

**Warhammer Fantasy Roleplay** is a tabletop roleplaying game, sometimes shortened to RPG or TTRPG, that combines elements of storytelling with board game mechanics. Most players will create a Character, one of the protagonists of the story. One player in your group will take on the role of Gamemaster (GM), who narrates the events and plays all of the other characters the players might meet.
If you are new to RPGs, you can find more information, free adventures, and other releases on our website, www.cubicle7games.com.
## **THROWING BONES**

Games of **Warhammer Fantasy Roleplay** use ten-sided dice marked from 0–9, where a roll of 0 counts as a result of 10. These are called d10s, and the number of dice to roll is shown as 1d10, 2d10, 3d10, and so on.
When rolling multiple dice, add the results together. For example, a roll of 0 and 3 on 2d10 gives a result of 13 (10 + 3).
Sometimes, a die roll will be modified by adding or subtracting a number. For example, 1d10+4 means roll one d10 and add 4, while 2d10-3 means roll two d10s, total the results, then subtract 3.

The rules also use 1d100, a roll from 1–100 made with two d10s. Designate one die as the tens die and the other as the units die, then read the results as a two-digit number. A 1 on the tens die and 4 on the units die gives 14; a 4 and 2 gives 42. If both dice roll 0, the result is 100.
In general, low rolls give successful results. So, whether you're rolling a d10 or a d100, you want to get as close to 01 as possible.
# **Using This Book**
You don't need to read this book cover to cover to get started. Depending on whether you intend to create a Character or GM a game for your friends, you may wish to vary your reading order.
- **Character Building:** A guide to making your Character
- **Careers:** Your Character's role in the world
- **Skills and Talents:** The abilities that make your Character stand out
- **Rules:** How to play the game
- **Between Adventures:** What happens when your Character is not adventuring
- **Religion:** The gods and how they influence the world
- **Magic:** Otherworldly forces wielded by witches and wizards
- **GM's Guide:** How to run games for your friends
- **Glorious Reikland:** A guide to the region most adventures take place in
- **Consumer Guide:** All of the weapons, armour, and other tools you will need
- **Bestiary:** Skulking cultists, hulking orcs, and other monsters to fight
# **Creating a Character**

**Chapter 2: Character Building** shows you how to create a hard-bitten soldier, furtive witch, or frothing flagellant and get started exploring the Old World. **Chapter 3: Careers** will tell you more about your Character's role in the world, and all of the Skills, Talents, and Trappings (gear) you can acquire. These are detailed more fully in **Chapter 4: Skills and Talents** and **Chapter 11: Consumers Guide**. **Chapter 7: Religion** and **Chapter 8: Magic** are essential reading if you want to call upon the power of the gods or the forces of magic.

**Chapter 10: Glorious Reikland** guides you through the region the game takes place in, its various locations, and what life there is like. **Chapter 6: Between Adventures** concerns everything your Character gets up to when they are not putting their life on the line for coin or glory.
You should avoid **Chapter 9** and **Chapter 12** until you are ready to GM games of your own.
# **Being a Gamemaster**

Familiarise yourself with **Chapter 10: Glorious Reikland**, to get a feel for the world and start planning your game. **Chapter 9: GM's Guide** gives advice on how to run fun and entertaining games, while **Chapter 12: Bestiary** contains a wide array of enemies and monsters for your players to encounter.
# **The Rules of the Road**

**Chapter 5: Rules** explains how the game actually works. For everything from fighting orcs to picking pockets, smooth-talking nobles to barrelling down cobbled streets in a break-neck chase, you'll find rules here on how to do it. It's important for both players and the Gamemaster to understand these rules in order to facilitate a smooth game.

in 2502 IC by the will of the elector counts and the blessings
of mighty Sigmar, rules with strength and wisdom that some
nevertheless deem insufficient to the task.
Welcome to Warhammer Fantasy Roleplay, a game like no
other. Here you will explore a world of glittering wonders, vile
darkness, and everything in between. You will encounter feared
and respected wizards who master their arts in the high towers of
the Colleges of Magic, as well as witches who dabble in magics
they barely understand. Priests, virtuous and fanatical in uneven
measure, preach the word of the gods and caution against dark
powers they fear to name. Proud ranks of soldiers march out
to cheers and wage war on orcs, beastmen, and other invaders.
They return scarred and diminished, or do not return at all.
Our protagonists are no heroes, assured of victory, gold, and
glory. What they would gain, they must win, often against the
odds, by strength, wit, and fortune. Coin is hard-earned and
quickly spent, and the most lucrative opportunities pit would-
be adventurers against hidden cults, bloodthirsty mercenaries,
or inhuman beasts that dwell in dark forests or deep beneath
the earth. Magic provides a powerful advantage, but it bears
risks of its own, and there is no pyre so well fed that a witch
hunter could not fit one more cur atop it. The gods heed the
prayers of their most faithful, but they are jealous and fickle,
quick to withdraw their blessing from those they no longer
consider worthy.
This book contains everything you need, aside from a few dice
and some paper and pencils. So gather your friends, appoint a
gamemaster, and prepare to explore the grim and perilous world
of Warhammer Fantasy Roleplay.
NEW TO ROLEPLAYING GAMES
Warhammer Fantasy Roleplay is a tabletop roleplaying game,
sometimes shortened to RPG or TTRPG, that combines
elements of storytelling with board game mechanics. Most
players will create a Character, one of the protagonists of
the story. One player in your group will take on the role of
Gamemaster (GM), who narrates the events and plays all of the
other characters the players might meet.
If you are new to RPGs, you can find more information,
free adventures, and other releases on our website,
www.cubicle7games.com.
THROWING BONES
Games of Warhammer Fantasy Roleplay use ten-sided dice
marked from 0–9, where a roll of 0 counts as a result of 10.
These are called d10s, and the number of dice to roll is shown
as 1d10, 2d10, 3d10, and so on.
When rolling multiple dice, add the results together. For
example, a roll of 0 and 3 on 2d10 gives a result of 13 (10 + 3).
Sometimes, a die roll will be modified by adding or subtracting
a number. For example, 1d10+4 means roll one d10 and add
4, while 2d10-3 means roll two d10s, total the results, then
subtract 3.
The rules also use 1d100, a roll from 1–100 made with two
d10s. Designate one die as the tens die and the other as the
units die, then read the results as a two-digit number. A 1 on
the tens die and 4 on the units die gives 14; a 4 and 2 gives 42.
If both dice roll 0, the result is 100.
In general, low rolls give successful results. So, whether you’re
rolling a d10 or a d100, you want to get as close to 01 as
possible.

## **APOTHECARY**
**Academic Class:** Dwarf, Halfling, High Elf, Human
*You use your knowledge of chemistry and concoction to mix and trade all manner of medicines and remedies.*

*'Fractured femur? I'll need a hare's gall bladder, sour milk, powdered limestone, nettle essence, and three days to prepare it. Drink daily at dawn and the bone should knit back together, but don't breathe on anyone you want to impress.'*
— Elvyra Jung, Apothecary

*'Manling remedies? As shoddy as their stonework! and just as likely to kill you! Asked for a tonic to cure this toothache. Had the flux for a week and my tooth is still throbbing like an apprentice's thumb!'*
— Thorica Norrasdottir, Dwarf Weaponsmith

Apothecaries specialise in preparing pills, draughts, and salves, substances created to affect the body in some way. While most of these preparations possess medicinal qualities, a skilled apothecary can also craft stimulants, poisons, and other compounds with dubious effects.

An Apothecary's workshop is filled with a dazzling array of bubbling alembics, overflowing crucibles, mortars and pestles, and other strange paraphernalia. Apothecaries may embark on expeditions to find exotic ingredients, to research new concoctions, or recover lost pharmacopoeia and forgotten formulae. They are valued travelling companions, not least for their skills as healers. Most physicians' guilds forbid Apothecaries from practising medicine in towns and cities, so an itinerant life often proves more lucrative.

Playing an Apothecary lets you heal or harm with equal skill. You can become an invaluable compatriot or a subtle danger to your enemies, thanks to your skill with poisons. You might grow rich selling your services on the road, find a noble patron who values your talents for good or ill, or dedicate yourself to discovering new ingredients and inventing new recipes.

Burgher Class: Dwarf, Halfling, Human
Charismatic and articulate, you champion your cause and try to change the world.
‘ALTDORF FOR ALTDORFERS! MIDDENLANDERS OUT!’
— Pamphlet, street of a Hundred Taverns, altdorf
‘Listen, if you’re looking to root out agents of the Spinner of Fate, follow the
clamour in the streets. They can’t resist it. They’ll surface, sooner or later.’
— Cleric-captain Wulfscheid, Knight of the Fiery Heart
and zealots as followers. Agitators who survive long enough to
become Demagogues are often supported by powerful, hidden allies
pursuing change for their own ends. Most Agitators are sincere in
their beliefs, though some are cynics and opportunists who exploit
discontent for personal gain.
Agitators champion political and religious causes using print,
protest, and public speaking. They muster the support of the
downtrodden, hoping the masses can force change. Whether they
call for the radical overthrow of the ruling classes or reactionary
support for the status quo, they stir up discontent against those
they blame for the world’s ills. The most successful Agitators have
destabilised the rule of nobles, towns, and even entire provinces.
Pamphleteers nail signs to billboards or distribute them in market
squares, though often those they seek to reach cannot read.
Religious Agitators can make a good living as street preachers,
receiving donations from pious devotees and attracting flagellants
Agitators often move around, in search of larger crowds or fleeing
the authorities. They may lead motley bands of the restless and
disaffected, exhorting them to fight for a greater cause. Some
Agitators travel from village to village, drumming up support, but
most are found in towns and cities where it is easier to sway crowds.
As an Agitator, you can sway crowds in your favour and help your
party negotiate the back and forth of city life, not to mention pick
(and hopefully win) an argument with almost anyone.

### **RIVERWOMAN**
**Riverfolk Class:** Dwarf, Halfling, Human
*You live with the ups and downs of life by the river, and the many interesting people who pass through.*
*'I don't care if you're a beggar or an elector count, if it wasn't for this river, there wouldn't even be an Empire.'*
— Greta Rutkinn, Stirgau Wharfinger

*'They say the whole Empire will eventually float by if you sit by the Reik long enough. Well, I've sat here, rod in hand, for twenty years, watching the flow downriver. The things I could tell you. I've seen war and I've seen peace. I've seen good times and bad. I've seen happiness and sorrow. And in all that time, I can honestly say, I've not caught a single bloody fish.'*
— Thys Lange, the Reikland's worst Fisherman

The Empire's great rivers support countless towns and villages whose people make their living from the water. Some Riverwomen fish with rod, spear, or net, others tend eel traps, dredge the riverbed, maintain wharfs, or build and repair boats. Wherever there is water, there is always work to be found.

Unlike inland villagers, those who live on great rivers are open and worldly, used to receiving outsiders who trade and restock at the wharfs. News from distant lands often reaches Riverwomen before anyone else.

A Riverwoman will feel at home on any stretch of water, and their skills ensure they can drop everything and find work away from home. Adventure makes an exciting change from mending nets, wading in mud, and wrestling fish from the water.

Playing a Riverwoman makes you a practical and dependable companion. Whether rowing a boat, finding food, repairing a net, or swapping stories with the locals, you can always earn your keep. Tough, resourceful, and at home on the water, you are well prepared for a life of adventure.

RIVERWARDEN
Riverfolk Class: Dwarf, Halfling, Human
Resolute and vigilant, you patrol the riverways in pursuit of lawbreakers and troublemakers.
‘The best patrol on the river is just past Two Tree Island. Almost nobody sails
down there and the fishing is excellent.’
— Haricot Chard, Halfling Riverwarden
‘Back when I was a Riverwarden, Big Willi came round and told me to leave
a certain shipment alone. Of course, I was young, wasn’t I? I told the ship’s
master all about it. And was I rewarded for my honesty? Nah, Big Willi beat
me up, and the next day I was drummed out of the river patrol.’
— nikki schnelling, Former river recruit
The Empire’s waterways are almost as perilous as its roads. River
pirates, wreckers, and worse dangers prey upon vessels of every
size, so the Imperial River Patrol keeps the major rivers safe for
trade and travel. It is a quasi-military force crewing large boats and
ships armed for a fight, the largest of which are protected by elite
Shipswords. More common are the small patrols that sail the rivers
looking for malefactors or innocent crews to sting with spurious
spot fines — which may line their own pockets. Other Riverwardens
serve ashore in lonely outposts overlooking strategically important
stretches of river.
A diligent Riverwarden searching vessels and following up leads
may stumble across any sort of nefarious plot or sinister cargo. Such
discoveries often lead to adventure, whether investigating with the
patrol’s blessing or accompanying others to protect the Empire’s
waterways.
Playing a Riverwarden combines the skills of a sailor, investigator,
and fighter. Boarding suspicious vessels, tracking down smugglers,
and defending honest travellers from pirates and monsters are all in
a day’s work on the Empire’s waterways.

### **Cat-tongued**
Like Ranald the Trickster God, you blend truth and lies as if there were no difference. You gain Advantage on any Charm Test you make to lie convincingly.
### **Chaos Magic (Lore)**

By accident or design, you have lost a portion of your soul to one of the Dark Gods, and can now practise the foul magics of Chaos. Your ruinous patron immediately grants you access to Spells from the chosen Chaos Lore. Upon learning the Talent, you gain one Spell of your choice from your chosen Lore. You may now memorise additional Spells from your chosen Lore for the following cost in XP.
Each time you obtain a Spell of your chosen Lore, you gain a Corruption Point as the spell infiltrates your mind, never to be forgotten.
Under normal circumstances, you may not learn more than one Lore of Chaos. Unlike the *Arcane Lore* Talent, once learned, this Talent may never be unlearned.

### **Combat Aware**

You are used to scanning the battlefield to make snap decisions informed by the shifting tides of war. You may take a **Challenging (+0 SL) Perception** Test to avoid gaining the *Surprised* Condition. If the GM would normally allow a Test to ignore Surprise in this circumstance, you automatically succeed.
### **Combat Master**

You are adept at making your presence felt on the battlefield, using your size or speed to corner your opponents. You count as two people for the purposes of outnumbering an opponent, or when determining if your side is outnumbered. See page 167 for the rules for outnumbering.
### **Combat Reflexes**
You react quickly to danger, leaping to attack your enemy without pause. When you roll for Combat Initiative, roll twice and choose your prefered result.
### **Commanding Presence**

Your presence inspires awe and admiration. In the absence of recognised authority, most people naturally look to you for leadership in a crisis and follow any reasonable orders you give. In addition, you gain Advantage on Leadership Tests.
### **Concoct**

You are skilled at making potions and draughts on the go. You may make a free *Crafting* Endeavour each session to use Trade (Apothecary, Herbalist, or Poisoner) without the need for a Workshop. Trade Tools and raw materials are still required. Due to the rushed nature of the creation, it expires at the start of the next Downtime, regardless of whether the item has been completed or not.
### **Contortionist**

You can bend and manipulate your body in a myriad of seemingly unnatural ways. This allows you to squeeze through gaps that would normally be difficult or impossible, at the GM's discretion. You gain Advantage on any Athletics Test made to escape from bonds.
### **Coolheaded**
Gain +5 Willpower. This does not count toward Advances.
### **Crack the Whip**

You know how to get the most out of your animals. Assuming you have the Drive Skill, you can direct your vehicle's animals to take an Action, as well as a Move, without a Test. When a Drive Test is required, make it with Advantage. When driving a vehicle in a Pursuit, add +1 to the animals' Movement Attributes.
### **Craftsman (Trade)**

You are a true creative talent, sufficiently skilled in a craft to have the potential to elevate it to an art form. Choose a Trade Specialisation. You gain Advantage on Tests of this skill, and may Advance it even if it is not part of your current Career. You may purchase this Talent more than once, choosing a new Trade Specialisation each time you do.
### **Criminal**

You are an active criminal making money from illegal sources, and you are not always quiet about it. When you successfully use the *Income* Endeavour to earn coin from a criminal enterprise of any kind, double the resulting coin.

on Athletics Tests made while falling.
Under normal circumstances, you may not learn more than one
Bless (Deity) Talent. Further, you may not learn the Channelling
Skill or the Arcane Magic, Chaos Magic, Magic Resistance, Petty
Magic, or Witch! Talents when you have the Bless Talent, and
vice versa. You can unlearn this Talent for 100 XP, but will lose
all of your Blessings if you do so, and may garner the disfavour of
the god you have spurned, with effects determined by your GM.
Bookish
You are an avid reader, and know how to quickly navigate your
way around a library. You gain Advantage on any Research
Test you make.
Break and Enter
Just by observing a building, locked room, or vault, you can
determine what looks to be the fastest and quietest route
in. Additionally, you have Advantage on Pick Lock Tests, or
Strength Tests made to force open doors or windows.
Briber
You need only share a few words with someone to know if they
are open to a bribe, and exactly how much would be required
to have them turn a blind eye, or even assist in some nefarious
activity. You have Advantage on any Bribery Test you make.
Cardsharp
You are used to playing, and winning, at games, although
your methods may involve a little cheating. When making an
Opposed Gamble Test, if you roll a double, you may reroll your
opponent’s Test. This additionally negates any benefit your
opponent may have gained with Sleight of Hand.
Careful Strike
You are skilled at hitting your enemy exactly where you want to.
When making a Melee Attack, the penalty for making a Called
Shot is reduced to -1 SL. If your attack is made with Advantage,
you may make a Called Shot at no penalty.
Carouser
You are a seasoned drinker and know how to party hard. You
do not suffer any ill effects from consuming modest amounts
of alcohol, and only need to make a Consume Alcohol Test if
drinking to excess — for example, if attempting to impress a bar
full of dwarfs. You gain Advantage on any Consume Alcohol
Test you make, as well as any Endurance Test you make to resist
the effects of poison.
Cat-tongued
Like Ranald the Trickster God, you blend truth and lies as if
there were no difference. You gain Advantage on any Charm
Test you make to lie convincingly.
Chaos Magic (Lore)
By accident or design, you have lost a portion of your soul to
one of the Dark Gods, and can now practise the foul magics of
Chaos. Your ruinous patron immediately grants you access to
Spells from the chosen Chaos Lore. Upon learning the Talent,
you gain one Spell of your choice from your chosen Lore. You
may now memorise additional Spells from your chosen Lore for
the following cost in XP.
Each time you obtain a Spell of your chosen Lore, you gain a
Corruption Point as the spell infiltrates your mind, never to be
forgotten.
Under normal circumstances, you may not learn more than one
Lore of Chaos. Unlike the Arcane Lore Talent, once learned, this
Talent may never be unlearned.
Combat Aware
You are used to scanning the battlefield to make snap
decisions informed by the shifting tides of war. You may take
a Challenging (+0 SL) Perception Test to avoid gaining the
Surprised Condition. If the GM would normally allow a Test to
ignore Surprise in this circumstance, you automatically succeed.
Combat Master
You are adept at making your presence felt on the battlefield,
using your size or speed to corner your opponents. You count as
two people for the purposes of outnumbering an opponent, or
when determining if your side is outnumbered. See page 167 for
the rules for outnumbering.

md: # **Stealth and Surveillance**
Moving unseen and spotting danger are valuable skills throughout the Empire. Here are some common situations and how to resolve them.
#### **Keeping an Eye Out**

If a Character is watching for threats or suspects they are being followed, make an Opposed Perception Test against the target's appropriate Stealth Skill. The GM should allow the Test even if no one is there — a little paranoia is often healthy.
#### **Casing the Joint**

To observe a location, make a **Challenging (+0 SL) Perception** Test. For each +SL, the GM reveals one useful fact, such as who comes and goes, how well the location is guarded, what lies inside, ways to enter or leave unseen, or whether anyone else is watching it.
#### **Sneaking Around**

To move unseen, make the appropriate Stealth Test (Rural, Underground, or Urban) opposed by the Perception of whoever you are trying to avoid. If there are multiple observers, use the highest Perception.
A suitable distraction, such as a modest fire, a street brawl, or a blathering guest (page 115), grants Advantage on Stealth Tests.
| COMMON FORMS OF SKULLDUGGERY | |
| Action | Test |
| Pick a pocket | A Sleight of Hand Test, opposed by your target's Perception. |
| Force open a door or window | A Strength Test to do it quickly, or a Stealth (Urban) Test with the right tools to do it quietly. |
| Pick a lock | A Pick Lock Test, with a difficulty set by the lock's quality. Especially challenging locks might require an Extended Test, with one roll every round, or every minute. |
| Connect with local criminals | A Difficult (-1 SL) Gossip Test, made with Advantage if you have the Criminal Talent yourself. |

| Argue your innocence | A Charm Test, opposed by your opponent's Cool, or an opposed Lore (Law) Test to do so in court. Either way, Test with Disadvantage if you were caught red-handed or if there is incriminating evidence. |
| Cheat at cards | A Sleight of Hand Test, opposed by your opponent's Perception. Success grants Advantage on your next Gamble Test during that game. |
| Bribe a guard | A Bribery Test to find someone open to being bribed, at a price set by their status. You might Haggle with them over the price. |
| Learn a thing's value | An Evaluate Test to learn something's value, or a Difficult (-1 SL) Evaluate Test to quickly spot the most valuable thing in a room. |
## **EXAMPLE DIFFICULTIES OF COMMON UNDERHANDED TASKS**
| Difficulty | Action |

| Very Easy (+6 SL) | Sleight of Hand: Steal bread from a helpless urchin.
Charm: Convince an already furious mob to set fire to something.
Bribe: Find a corrupt tax inspector on the docks in Übersreik. |

| Easy (+4 SL) | Stealth (Urban): Vanish into a crowded street at night.
Lore (Law): Explain you can't be arrested solely for looking suspicious.
Intimidate: Threaten a common thief into bothering someone less well-armed. |

| Average (+2 SL) | Sleight of Hand: Run a common scam, like cups or Manaan's Shells.
Perception: Spot an ogre moving through a nearby street.
Gossip: Find the name of a wealthy merchant or other tempting mark. |

| Challenging (+0 SL) | Gamble: Win a few shillings gambling with bored merchants.
Charm: Have a gang of thieves agree to teach you the ropes.
Stealth (Rural): Sneak into a noble's country manor. |

| Difficult (-1 SL) | Evaluate: Spot the one true masterpiece amid a selection of forgeries.
Intimidate: Convince a dwarf to pay protection money.
Charm: Convince an angry mob to set fire to someone. |

| Hard (-2 SL) | Lore (Law): Convince a Witch Hunter to respect your Wizard's Licence.
Gossip: Spread a rumour that a famous knight has one wooden leg.
Charm: Trick a merchant into buying a bridge from you. |

| Very Hard (-3 SL) | Intimidate: Convince a Shallyan nun to abandon her patient.
Bribe: Convince a Captain of the Reiksguard to look the other way.
Charm: Convince an angry mob to calm down and hear you out. |
#### **EXAMPLE OUTCOMES**
**A Stealth (Rural) Test to infiltrate a guarded manor house.**
**Astounding Success (+5 SL):** You sneak inside and happen upon a servant's livery drying on the line — the perfect disguise should you wish to explore the living quarters.
**Impressive Success (+3 to +4 SL):** You sneak inside and notice a poorly guarded garden path you can later use to make a quick escape.
**Success (+1 to +2 SL):** You sneak inside the manor without being seen.
**Marginal Success (+0 SL):** You sneak inside, but leave signs of your entrance that will surely be noticed come morning.
**Marginal Failure (-0 SL):** You fail to find a safe way inside, but manage to avoid being spotted by the guards during your attempt.
**Failure (-1 to -2 SL):** You're discovered by a guard who spots you from across the courtyard. Time to run!
**Impressive Failure (-3 to -4 SL):** You stumble into the path of a patrol, who bellow a warning to the estate before drawing the blades and bearing down on you.
**Astounding Failure (-5 SL):** A misplaced step sees you tumbling from a watch house roof and right into the path of the captain of the guards, who recognises you on the spot.

Silent Takedowns
To silently subdue an unaware guard or sentry, make an Opposed
Melee Test against the target’s Endurance. If the attacker wins,
they inflict damage equal to their Strength Bonus and the target
gains the Unconscious Condition.
If the target wins, they instead gain the Stunned Condition and
immediately raise the alarm.
Characters with the Strike to Stun Talent gain Advantage on
this Test. Silent Takedowns can only be attempted outside
combat against unaware targets.
gamBling and CheaTing
To resolve a game of chance, make an Opposed Gamble Test.
The character with the highest SL wins.
To cheat, make a Sleight of Hand Test opposed by the highest
Perception among your opponents. Success grants Advantage
on your next Gamble Test in that game. Failure usually means
you are caught.
Use these rules only when the outcome of the game is important
to the adventure. Routine gambling for income is best handled
with the Income Endeavour (page 199).

precedente: THEFT AND SKULLDUGGERY
Crime is common in the Empire. Some say anything not nailed
down is likely to be stolen, but that overlooks the thriving
second-hand market for questionably acquired nails.
Characters are likely to break the law from time to time,
often for good reason. A crime may even be the focus of an
adventure, such as breaking into a wealthy merchant’s home
to uncover evidence of cult activity. In such cases, every detail
matters, from breaking in and searching for hidden evidence to
escaping unseen.
There is often no need to make a Test when time is not an issue
or failure has few consequences. For example, if the players steal
a locked chest, you can simply say they force it open once they
have time, rather than requiring a Pick Lock Test.
A TIME FOR CRIME
If a Character earns their living through crime, such as a Thief
or Charlatan, treat it like any other Career. Their routine work
is resolved during Downtime using the Income endeavour.
There is no need to roleplay picking the pocket of every NPC
they encounter — that would quickly become frustrating for the
other players!

md: | Law | Know what the law is and how it might be broken or circumvented, and make a compelling legal argument or recognise the flaw in one. |

| Magic | Recall the names of the Winds of Magic and their effects, recognise the trappings of a particular magical tradition, or determine if a grimoire contains true spells or the ravings of the mad. |
| Metallurgy | Determine what metals or alloys a weapon or tool is made of, how it was likely to have been forged, and how it might be repaired. |
| Science | Knowledge of natural philosophy — how the mundane phenomena appear to work, and the theory behind creating unusual compounds such as black powder or soap. |
| Theology | The practices and beliefs behind religions common to your culture, such as Sigmar, Taal, or Ulric, worshipped in the Empire, or Asuryan and Khaine, who are revered by the elves. |

A Character's Lore Specialisations represent their knowledge. If you have at least one Advance in an appropriate Lore, you automatically know basic facts about that subject. For example, a Character with Lore (Reikland) simply knows that the Reikland is a province of the Empire. Make a Lore Test only to recall unusual, obscure, or hidden information.

The more specific a Lore skill is to the question at hand, the more nuanced and detailed the information learned. For example, an **Average (+2 SL) Lore (Empire)** Test is sufficient to learn exactly where Helmgart is, while an **Average (+2 SL) Lore (Helmgart) Test** would reveal where it is, who rules it, the names of some prominent individuals there, and so on.
Lore represents theoretical knowledge about a subject, while Trade represents putting that knowledge into practice.
#### **Language**

Every Character speaks their native language fluently and does not need a Language Skill to use it. A Language Test is required only to convey especially complex ideas, understand obscure vocabulary or dialects, or pass as a native speaker. Once you have 4 Advances (+20) in a Language Specialisation, you speak that language fluently and no longer need to make Language Tests in most cases.
#### **Language Specialisations**

Some languages belong to the same family. Native speakers of one can usually hold a basic conversation with speakers of a related language, even without the appropriate Language Skill. They cannot read or write it, pass as a native speaker, or reliably understand complex ideas or unfamiliar vocabulary until they learn the Skill.
### **BATTLE TONGUE**

Battle Tongue is a specialised language that conveys complex tactical information in just a few words. A Character who passes a **Challenging (+0 SL) Language (Battle)** Test can use their Action to communicate up to 40 words of orders or tactical advice to others who know Language (Battle).
If players spend too long discussing tactics during combat, the GM can remind them that only Characters with Battle Tongue can exchange detailed plans in the heat of battle.
The following are the most common languages of the Old World, and the peoples who speak them. Many other tongues exist, but these are the ones most often encountered in the Reikland.
| LANGUAGE | FAMILY | SPOKEN BY… |
| Albion | None | …the folk of Albion, who hail from a far-off, mist shrouded island realm and are rarely encountered. |
| Battle Tongue | None | …warriors of the Old World. Composed of simple commands and gestures, it was supposedly developed by the goddess Myrmidia when she walked the Old World as a mortal. |
| Bretonnian | Haffennaff, Reikspiel, Wastelander | …the folk of Bretonnia, a chivalric realm to the southwest of the Empire. |
| Classical | Estalian, Tilean | …Human academics of all kinds. Over 3,000 years old, it is used in most scholarly texts of the Empire, including grimoires and many holy books. |
| Elthárin | None | …the folk of Athel Loren, the Laurelorn, and visiting merchants from Ulthuan. The tonal language has many dialects, and is notoriously difficult for non-elves to learn. |
| Estalian | Classical, Tilean | …the folk of Estalia, people of the hot, southwestern kingdoms known for their bitter politics and worship of the goddess Myrmidia. |

| Gospodarinyi | Górelsk, Ungol | …the majority of the folk of Kislev, a hardy people from the frozen oblasts to the east of the Empire. The language is often called Kislevarin or Kislevite by outsiders. |
| Grumbarth | None | …ogres. Few others learn this simple tongue, though some mercenary commanders find it useful. |
| Guilder | None | …members of appropriate trade guilds. Guilder is a slang-rich patois used to protect trade secrets and reinforce bonds. |
| Haffennaff | Bretonnian, Reikspiel, Wastelander | …the folk of the Mootland, the halfling grand province in the Empire. Also called Mootish. |
| Khazalid | None | …the folk of Karaz Ankor, the dwarf kingdoms in the mountains. This language is also widespread through the Cult of Sigmar, in honour of Sigmar's friendship with the dwarfs. |
| Magick | None | …spellcasters. A catch-all term for tonal languages used to shape the Winds of Magic into material effects. Magick is not used for communication. |
| Norse | None | …the folk of Norsca. Norse is commonly spoken across the north of the Empire in Nordland and Ostland, and is well-known in the Wasteland and Kislev, too. |
| Pilgrim Sign | None | …pilgrims and holy folk of the Old World who have taken vows of silence. This is a sign language with a full vocabulary, often learned by deaf folk. |

| Reikspiel | Bretonnian, Haffennaff, Wastelander | …the folk of the Empire. Reikspiel is the primary language used in most WFRP games. It is the modern version of the tongue once spoken by the god-king Sigmar. |
| Queekish | None | …the folk of the Under-empire. Used by the skaven. |
| Tilean | Classical, Estalian | …the folk of Tilea, who are most commonly encountered in the Empire as traders or mercenaries. |
| Thieves Tongue | None | …street folk of the Old World. Expressions of this language are highly localised and individual, with local variants common. |

| Wastelander | Bretonnian, Haffennaff, Reikspiel | ...the rural folk of the Wasteland, a windswept territory to the west of the Reikland. The official language of the Wasteland's capital, Marienburg, is Reikspiel, a reminder that the nation was once part of the Empire. |

who are revered by the elves.

md: # **INJURY, HEALING, AND DEATH**
Getting hurt is all but unavoidable. Combat, accidents, spells gone awry, and simple bad luck can all lead to lost Wounds, hideous infections, or an untimely trip to the Garden of Morr.
# **Wounds**

Wound loss represents minor cuts, bruises, and depleted reserves of energy. Wounds are lost by sustaining Damage (page 164). The lowest number of Wounds you can ever have is 0. If you would be taken to negative Wounds, you instead suffer a Critical Wound.
# **Healing Wounds**

At the end of each day, make an **Average (+2 SL) Endurance** Test. If successful, you recover Wounds equal to the SL + your Toughness Bonus. If the day was spent restfully, you recover a further number of Wounds equal to your Toughness Bonus even if you failed this Test.
#### **Using the Heal Skill**

You, or another Character, can use the Heal skill to recover more Wounds, so long as they have access to bandages, poultices, or other medical supplies. A successful Heal Test recovers Intelligence Bonus + SL Wounds. The difficulty of the Test is determined by the circumstances and the nature of the injury — during Combat it is never easier than Challenging (+0 SL). A patient can only benefit from one Heal roll per incident in which they lost Wounds, such as a fight, fall, or unfortunate accident involving the graf 's horse.
A fumbled Heal Test inflicts 1d10 Wounds, but cannot reduce the target below 1 Wound.
#### **THE HEAL SKILL AND BLEEDING CONDITIONS**

Characters remove one *Bleeding* Condition for each Wound they recover. While the Heal Skill can only be used to recover Wounds once per incident, you can still use it to remove *Bleeding* Conditions — simply remove one for each Wound that would have been recovered.
#### **HEALING ANIMALS**
When attempting to heal an animal, follow the rules for healing as laid out here but replace the Heal Skill with the Animal Care Skill.
# **OPEN WOUNDS**

If you lose Wounds and do not apply a Bandage (page 316) or have your injury seen to in some other way, such as by a successful use of the Heal Skill, you risk infection. At the end of the day, make an **Average (+ 2 SL) Endurance** Test. If you fail, you incur the *Infection* Symptom (page 182) until you are treated with a successful **Difficult (-1 SL) Heal** Test, or obtain a herbal Remedy (page 314) or other suitable cure.
# **Magic, Alchemy, and Healing**
Spells, Blessings, and some rare concoctions (page 314) can also heal Wounds, though such means are all either rare, expensive, or both.
# **Critical Wounds**
Critical Wounds are severe, and include broken bones, torn muscles, internal injuries, and sundered flesh. Critical Wounds are debilitating and dangerous. Gain too many and you risk death.
There are two ways to receive a Critical Wound. One is to suffer a Critical Hit, the other is to incur any Damage that would reduce your Wounds below 0.
#### **Inflicting Critical Wounds on an Opponent with 0 Wounds**

If Damage would reduce a character to below 0 Wounds, instead reduce them to 0 Wounds and inflict a Critical Wound. Roll a d100 on the relevant **Critical Wounds** table for the struck Location (pages 173–176). When rolling on the **Critical Wounds** table, add +10 to the result for every Wound inflicted beyond what was needed to reduce them to 0 Wounds.
#### **Inflicting Critical Wounds with Critical Hits**
Any Critical on a Melee or Ranged Test, whether attacking or defending, is a Critical Hit and inflicts a Critical Wound.

For a Critical Wound caused by a Critical Hit, do not reverse your attack roll to find out the Location of your strike as you would do for a normal hit. Instead, roll a d100 again to work out where your hit landed (see page 164), then roll a d100 again on the relevant **Critical Wounds** table for that Location.

> Attack Tests that both result in a Critical Hit and which inflict Damage that would reduce Wounds below zero inflict two Critical Wounds — one inflicted to a hit location determined by reversing the roll, and an additional one inflicted to a random hit location, as explained above.
# **PULLING YOUR BLOWS**

PULLING YOUR BLOWS
The rules assume you wish to inflict every possible Critical
Wound you can. It is also possible you may just want to subdue,
not kill, your opponents — or you may be sparring. With that
in mind, you may ignore any Critical Wound you should inflict
upon your opponents if you declare you are ‘pulling your blow’
before you roll to hit. If you do this, make sure you describe
the situation appropriately, making it clear you are using the flat
of your blade or otherwise doing what you can to avoid properly
hurting your opponent.
You may not pull blows with missiles, spells, Miracles, or
weapons that cause Ablaze Conditions. The following Weapon
Qualities are lost when pulling your blows: Damaging, Hack,
Impact, Impale, and Penetrating.
If you are trying to knock your opponent out you will need to:
1. Declare your intention and that you are pulling your
blows.
2. Hit them on the Head location.
3. use a weapon with the Pummel Quality.
Inflict more Stunned Conditions than your target’s
Toughness Bonus.
Or use the silent Takedown rules (page 135).
Additional Wound Loss from Critical Wounds
Use the Wounds column on the Critical Wounds table to
determine additional Wounds lost as a result of that Critical
Wound. Work out this extra damage after calculating all other
effects of normal damage and Critical Wounds. Wounds
caused in this way do not cause further rolls on the Critical
Wounds table.

precedente: Exposure
Every 4 hours spent in a difficult environment — such as
subzero temperatures, a hot desert, or a howling storm —
requires you to take an Endurance Test. Extreme environments
require a Test every 2 hours.
Cold: Your first failure inflicts Disadvantage on Tests based
on Ballistic Skill, Agility, and Dexterity. The second failure
inflicts Disadvantage on all Tests. Subsequent failures cause
1d10 Damage, ignoring Armour Points. If you reach 0 Wounds,
you do not suffer a Critical Wound, but immediately take the
Unconscious Condition. You will die in Toughness Bonus hours
unless you are somehow warmed up. Certain Trappings may
provide bonuses or penalties to these Tests, for example a coat
(page 309).
Heat: Your first failure inflicts Disadvantage on Tests based on
Intelligence and Willpower, and adds a Fatigued Condition.
The second failure inflicts Disadvantage on all Tests, and adds
another Fatigued Condition. Subsequent failures cause 1d10
Damage ignoring Armour Points. If you reach 0 Wounds,
you do not suffer a Critical Wound, but immediately take the
Unconscious Condition. You will die in Toughness Bonus hours
unless you are somehow cooled off. Stripping off all armour
grants +1 SL on Endurance Tests to resist exposure to heat.
Thirst and Starvation
Running out of provisions can be bad. Running out of water is
worse. Endurance Tests to withstand thirst and hunger become
increasingly difficult (cumulative -1 SL for each Test after the
first). Characters without food and water cannot heal Wounds
or recover Fatigued naturally.
Water: Every day without water requires you to take an
Endurance Test. The first failed Test inflicts Disadvantage on
Tests based on Intelligence, Willpower, and Fellowship. Second
and subsequent failures inflict Disadvantage on all Tests, and
cause 1d10 Damage ignoring Armour Points. If you reach 0
Wounds, you do not suffer a Critical Wound, but reduce your
Movement to 1, and you will die in Toughness Bonus days,
unless you get something to drink.
Food: Every 2 days without food requires an Endurance Test.
The first failed Test inflicts Disadvantage on Tests based on
Strength and Toughness. Second and subsequent failures inflict
Disadvantage on all Tests, and cause 1d10 Damage ignoring
Armour Points. If you reach 0 Wounds, you do not suffer a
Critical Wound, but permanently reduce your Toughness by
1d10. See Characteristic Loss, page 177.

md: Conditions represent the effects of things that can happen to you in the course of your adventures. The Conditions you suffer from can be recorded on a scrap sheet of paper, or you can use chits or counters to represent them. Each Condition explains how long any effects usually last in its description; however, it is possible the cause of a Condition — such as a Spell or Critical Wound — may override this.
When you incur a Condition, you immediately lose Momentum. You can still gain Momentum while suffering from one, unless the Condition states otherwise.
# **Multiple Conditions**

You can be subject to the same Condition more than once; indeed, sometimes you will receive multiples of the same Condition from a single event. If this occurs, any penalties suffered are stacked. So, if you have 3 *Bleeding* Conditions, you are losing a worrying 3 Wounds per Round; or if you have 3 *Fatigued* Conditions, you suffer -3 SL to all Tests.

You can also be subject to multiple, different Conditions at once. When this occurs, the effects do not stack; you suffer the highest of the two penalties and apply it. So, if you had 1 *Fatigued* and the *Prone* Condition, you would suffer a -2 SL penalty to all active Tests, not -3 SL.
# **COMPLETE CONDITION LIST**
- *Ablaze*
- *Besmirched*
- *Bleeding*
- *Blinded*
- *Broken*
- *Deafened*
- *Entangled*
- *Fatigued*
- *Poisoned*
- *Prone*
- *Stunned*
- *Surprised*
- *Unconscious*
#### **CONDITIONS AND FORTUNE**
A Condition can be removed with a Fortune Point, so while they are debilitating, they can be managed if you are careful (see page 133).
# **Master Condition List**
# **Ablaze**

You are on fire! This Condition is normally applied only to flammable creatures, such as those wearing combustible clothing, though some magical and divine effects can set even the non-flammable ablaze.

At the end of each Round, you suffer 1d10 Damage, reduced by your Toughness Bonus and the Armour Points on the least protected Hit Location. Each additional *Ablaze* Condition adds +1 Damage, so three *Ablaze* Conditions inflict 1d10 + 2 Damage. If this reduces you to 0 Wounds, you suffer a Critical Wound to the Body.

A successful Athletics Test removes 1 *Ablaze* Condition, and one more for each SL after the first. The GM modifies the Test's Difficulty to reflect the circumstances — for example, smothering flames in sand is much easier than in an oil-soaked kitchen.
# **Besmirched**

You are covered in effluent, foetid blood, troll mucus, or some other foul substances. More than merely treading in rat droppings or staining your jerkin with food, to be *Besmirched* is to be saturated in noxious gunk. Until you have a chance to clean yourself, you suffer Disadvantage to all Fellowship Tests.
This Condition does not stack — you are either *Besmirched* or you are not, so you do not collect multiple *Besmirched* Conditions.
# **Bleeding**

You are bleeding badly. Lose 1 Wound at the end of every Round, ignoring Toughness Bonus and Armour Points. If you reach 0 Wounds, you no longer lose Wounds; instead, at the end of each Round, make a **Challenging (+0 SL) Endurance** Test to avoid falling *Unconscious*.

If you are *Unconscious*, *Bleeding*, and at 0 Wounds, then at the end of each Round roll a d10. If the result is equal to or less than the number of *Bleeding* Conditions you have, you die. If you roll a 10, remove one *Bleeding* Condition. You cannot wake up until all *Bleeding* Conditions are removed.

For each Wound you recover by any means, remove a *Bleeding* Condition. A **Challenging (+0 SL) Heal** Test removes Intelligence Bonus + SL *Bleeding* Conditions. Applying a Bandage requires an Action, but no Test, and removes one *Bleeding* Condition — you may apply a Bandage as part of a Heal Test, even if the Test fails.
#### **Blinded**

Because of a powerful flash of light, blood in your eyes, or a terrible wound, you cannot see, and cannot undertake any task that requires sight, such as reading or making Ranged Attacks. You suffer Disadvantage to Melee Attacks and other Tests that rely heavily on sight but do not strictly require it, such as Climb or Ride. Melee Attacks against you benefit from Advantage, unless your foe is also *Blinded.*

> Normally, one *Blinded* Condition is removed at the end of your Turn. However, if you have received a *Blinded* Condition as a result of imbibing a poison or an injury, it may persist for a longer period.
#### **Broken**

precedente: Frenzy
You can work yourself into a frothing rage by howling like a wolf,
flaying strips of sinful skin from your unworthy flesh, or simply
embracing the deep well of bloodlust within. On your Turn, you
may enter a state of Frenzy by passing a Willpower Test.
While subject to Frenzy, you are immune to all other Psychology,
may make an extra Melee Attack as a Free Action each round,
and inflict +1 Damage on all Melee Attacks.
While in this murderous state, you must move towards your
nearest foe and attack them. You may only use your Move or
Action to further this goal. You remain in Frenzy until all nearby
foes are bested, or you become Stunned or fall Unconscious.
After your Frenzy is over, you immediately receive a Fatigued
Condition.
Hatred (Target)
You bear a burning hatred towards the Target, usually a group
of people or creatures, such as ‘Hochlanders’, ‘Bog Octopuses’,
or ‘Goblins’. You can never socially interact with that group,
save perhaps to bellow a blood oath of vengeance as you ready
your axe for the slaughter. Each time you encounter them, you
must pass a Psychology Test or be compelled to destroy the
hated group by the fastest and most deadly means possible.
Once you have slain your foe or driven them off, you calm
down sufficiently to consider other courses of action. If you
wish to restrain yourself prior to this, you may attempt another
Psychology Test at the end of each round after the first.
You always gain a bonus of +1 SL on Melee and Ranged Tests
against the specified group, and are immune to Intimidate and
Fear (but not Terror) caused by your hated foe, even if you have
passed a Psychology Test to control your Hatred.
Terror (Rating)
Some creatures are so profoundly unsettling as to provoke a
dire, bone-chilling terror in their foes. When you first encounter
a creature causing Terror, make a Psychology Test unless they
are a known ally. If you pass, you suffer no further effects of
any Terror for the rest of the encounter. If you fail, you receive
a number of Broken Conditions equal to the creature’s Terror
Rating, plus one more for every negative SL after the first.
When encountering multiple sources of Terror, this test is made
against the highest Terror Rating among them.
After resolving the Psychology Test, the creature causes Fear,
with a Fear Rating equal to their Terror Rating.

md: # **HALFLING GODS**

Some say that halflings are superstitious rather than religious, and the bulk of their deities support this impression. Most halfling gods and goddesses have to do with hearth and home, cooking, herblore, earthy matters, and general day-to-day concerns. Halfling gods are practical rather than philosophical; as the saying goes, 'Deep thoughts butter no parsnips'. Halflings also show respect to certain human deities, Sigmar, Taal, and Rhya in particular, but this is more from a desire to avoid conflict than from any sincere devotion.
# **Halfling Priests**

Halflings do not really have priests, and they certainly do not build temples (though humans seem happy to do it for them, especially Sigmarites). There are better things to do than warble on about someone else's business. Of course, they respect the gods, and have shrines on-hand should they need to have a quick natter, but none make a career exclusively talking to just one god — why make yourself so exclusive? Should a particular god need to be appeased, it is usually left up to a local elder to do what is required on behalf of the community, often after a great deal of talking with relevant experts and peers.
