DWARF ANCESTOR GODS
The dwarfs venerate their ancient ancestors, valuing tradition
above all else. Though the Time of the Ancestor Gods was many
thousands of years ago (roughly –5500 IC as scholars reckon it),
the dwarfs still hold records of that time in their oldest holds.
Many names echo from that era, creating a broad, inter-related
pantheon, but three ancestor gods are of especial importance
and are known by all dwarfs: Grimnir, Grungni, and Valaya,
each a progenitor of the species as a whole.
In addition to the oldest ancestor gods, dwarfs also revere the
founders of local clans as guardian deities.
Dwarf Priests
Those dedicating themselves to the cults of the ancestor gods
do not use the Nun, Priest, or Warrior Priest Careers, as dwarfs
have a very different relationship with their gods, seeking to
emulate them rather than worship or appease them.
Because of this, if you wish to play a dwarf dedicated to one
of the ancestor gods, simply choose an appropriate Career to
best act like that god. So, if you wanted to emulate Grimnir,
effectively becoming a priest of Grimnir, perhaps play a Slayer
and join the Cult of the Slayer, or maybe become a Soldier.
elven gods
The elves worshipped their own gods long before humans
and most other species existed in their current forms. Their
pantheon is extensive, with different groups of deities being
held as important by wood elves and high elves.
The elves recognise two groups of gods: the Cadai and
the Cytharai. The Cadai rule the heavens, and have strong
connections to their elven worshippers, directly helping where
they can. The selfish Cytharai rule the underworld, and care
little for the elves. Standing apart from both these courts are
a loose group of unaligned gods, including Ellinill, the Lord of
Destruction, and several of his fugitive children.
The high elves especially revere the Cadai, and have sophisticated
priesthoods dedicated to their teachings. They appease the
Cytharai when necessary, but it is considered dangerous and
distasteful to court them too openly or readily. According to
their myths, Asuryan, the god of creation, is king of all the gods,
able to pronounce judgement upon them all.
The wood elves take a much more balanced approach and have
temples and shrines to all the gods impacting their lives, be they
Cadai or Cytharai. Because of their close association with the
woods and forests, they revere Isha the Mother and Kurnous
the Hunter above all others, and rumours persist that both gods
take a direct hand in wood elf affairs.
According to elven theologians, the deities of this pantheon are
the true gods, and those worshipped by other species are simply
pale reflections of the elven originals.
Elven Priests
Both high elves and wood elves have priesthoods for the gods,
but they do not have Blessings and Miracles. Elves do not
believe the gods manifest in this fashion, and instead see magic
as a gift from the gods. Because of this, if you wish to be an elven
priest, use the Wizard Career, and choose from an appropriate
Lore to represent the magic your god has gifted you. So, a priest
of Kurnous would specialise in the Lore of Beasts, a worshipper
of Isha in the Lore of Life, and devotees of Asuryan in the Lore
of Light or Fire.
HALFLING GODS
Some say that halflings are superstitious rather than religious,
and the bulk of their deities support this impression. Most
halfling gods and goddesses have to do with hearth and home,
cooking, herblore, earthy matters, and general day-to-day
concerns. Halfling gods are practical rather than philosophical;
as the saying goes, ‘Deep thoughts butter no parsnips’. Halflings
also show respect to certain human deities, Sigmar, Taal, and
Rhya in particular, but this is more from a desire to avoid
conflict than from any sincere devotion.
Halfling Priests
Halflings do not really have priests, and they certainly do not
build temples (though humans seem happy to do it for them,
especially Sigmarites). There are better things to do than warble
on about someone else’s business. Of course, they respect the
gods, and have shrines on-hand should they need to have a
quick natter, but none make a career exclusively talking to just
one god — why make yourself so exclusive? Should a particular
god need to be appeased, it is usually left up to a local elder to
do what is required on behalf of the community, often after a
great deal of talking with relevant experts and peers.
VII

md: # **The Lore of Life**

The Lore of Life relates to *Ghyran*, the Jade Wind. Free flowing *Ghyran* is associated with growth, fertility, and nourishment. To those with the Sight, *Ghyran* appears much like a light rain, falling to the ground and pooling in eddying swirls. It sinks into the soil and is drawn up into the roots of plants from where it goes on to nourish all living things. The druids of the Jade Order often prefer life away from the cities, attuned to the seasons and the natural world.

Spells from the Lore of Life commonly involve healing and rejuvenation, from healing wounds to causing a barren field to burst with life. They can have offensive applications, too. The enemies of a druid may find themselves suddenly tangled up in wickedly sharp brambles and vines.
#### **The Lore of Heavens**

The Lore of Heavens relates to *Azyr*, the Blue Wind. It cascades through the skies over the Old World, crackling through the heavens, like a great, charged cloud. Astromancers of the Celestial Order, known for their calm and contemplative manners, use the wind to scry the future, the lens of *Azyr* Spells from the Lore of Heavens involve the manipulation of fate, throwing up protective barriers, or cursing a foe with an unnatural run of bad luck. On the battlefield, astromancers also control elemental forces, blasting their enemies with bolts of lightning, or even drawing down shooting stars from the heavens.
### **The Lore of Shadows**

The Lore of Shadows relates to *Ulgu*, the Grey Wind. To the Sight, it appears a thick fog, gathering in pools wherever intrigue and deceit are practised, rising into great storms and tempests when conflict breaks out. Wizards of the Grey Order, known as grey guardians, are secretive in their ways and given to uncertain loyalties. Despite this, the Grey Order is renowned for its wisdom and skill in negotiations, and is often called upon for diplomatic missions.

Spells from the Lore of Shadows can be used to mask or obfuscate, confusing and disorienting their foes. In battle, the shadowy, insubstantial tendrils of *Ulgu* they wield can pierce to the heart of their foes, eviscerating the most well-protected troops, yet leaving armour eerily intact.
#### **The Lore of Death**

The Lore of Death relates to *Shyish*, the Purple Wind. It is attracted to places of death, such as battlefields, gardens of Morr, and sites of execution. The wind is said to blow strongest during times of transition, so wizards of the Amethyst Order tend to work their greatest rites during the hours of twilight. While *Shyish* is related to time and mortality, it is distinct from Necromancy, the illegal practice of raising and binding the dead, which uses the Dark Magic of *Dhar* in lieu of *Shyish*. Indeed, the Amethyst Order, much like the Cult of Morr, works tirelessly to combat the threat of Necromancy.

Nevertheless, spells from the Lore of Death resemble Necromancy to the untrained eye. They can drain their targets of life force, spread fear among their enemies, and contact the spirits of the departed.
### **The Lore of Fire**

The Lore of Fire relates to *Aqshy*, the Red Wind. *Aqshy* is a hot and searing wind associated with brashness, courage, and zeal and is drawn to empirical heat. The pyromancers of the Bright Order are bold and hot-tempered and make for impressively destructive battle wizards.

Many of the spells from the Lore of Fire are offensive in nature, enabling the caster to conjure up great balls of fire, or cause the blades of their allies to burst into flame. Even their non-offensive spells, such as crude healing magics, are still destructive in nature. Bright wizards are also adept at inspiring their allies, rallying their courage and inspiring bravery and loyalty in the troops with which they serve.
#### **The Lore of Beasts**

The Lore of Beasts relates to *Ghur*, the Amber Wind, a cold, primal force associated with the savage wilds and the beasts living there. To those with the Sight, *Ghur* seems to blow weakly in areas where the wilderness has been tamed and settlements constructed. This may explain why the shamans of the Amber Order often take up a hermitic existence and shun their fellow Men.

The spells of the Lore of Beasts allow a shaman to communicate with animals, request their aid, and even summon them to battle. Shapeshifting magic may also be used by the wizard to adopt animal forms.
# **Elven Magic**

md: Elves can be encountered in the Empire, but are a rare sight and very much hold themselves apart from other species. An elf abroad in the Empire might be tasked with gathering information for their homeland and attach themselves to a band of adventurers to further this goal. Their long lives and appreciation of art might see an elf spend years accompanying an Artisan, Entertainer, or similar to witness their talent. They may even align themselves with a band of scoundrels out of a sense of adventure, or simple curiosity.

Knowing, vaguely, what sorts of adventures you intend to run will help your players make useful choices — so it is a good idea to let them in on a few details in advance, such as if their Characters will be wandering about or staying in one general area of the Old World for a time
# **Using the Rules**
Most of what you need to know about the rules can be found in **Chapter 5**, but there are a few that the GM needs to understand in a slightly more in-depth way than players.
#### **Fate and Fortune**

Fortune can turn a disastrous situation in your Characters' favour, so make spending it feel like a meaningful choice. When a Character considers spending Fortune, ask whether they are really sure they want to use it now, or whether they might need it more later. Conversely, if they have Fortune left unused, you can ask whether they want to spend it, implying that the situation may be more dangerous than it first appears. These moments should add drama to the decision without misleading the players, making the choice to spend Fortune feel like a moment of consequence rather than simply another resource.

Fate is another matter entirely. Spending Fate is a Big Deal: it is powerful enough to cheat death. When a Character spends Fate to survive, consider when they made the decision. If they spend it before Damage is rolled (**How Did That Miss?**), their escape can seem almost miraculously fortunate. They slip and the decapitating strikes whistles harmlessly overhead or an arrow rebounds off a Sigmarite medallion. If they use Fate after seeing the result, in order to avoid death (**Not Today!**), make their survival more desperate. Perhaps they are knocked unconscious and only awaken after the battle, or are swept into fast-moving water and carried a mile downstream before reaching the bank. If they spend Fate to achieve the impossible (**I Will Not Fail!**), describe how they tap into previously unknown reserves of strength to hold the portcullis up long enough for their companions to roll under, or how the grappling hook wedges improbably in a crack of the wall, allowing them to climb up just as the beastmen round the corner. Spending Fate should always feel like a dramatic moment in the adventure.

Regaining Fate should be rare enough to feel momentous, perhaps marking the culmination of a long campaign or the achievement of an objective at considerable personal cost. Fortune, by contrast, is replenished at the start of every session. This assumes a session of around four hours. For longer sessions, replenish Fortune at narratively appropriate moments, roughly every four hours. For shorter sessions, replenish it every other session to maintain a similar level of challenge.
#### **Opposed Tests**

Something should always happen as a result of an Opposed Test. Even when both Characters achieve the same SL and the Test ends in a stalemate, use the result to point towards a way forward. Perhaps neither side gains the upper hand, but one notices a weakness, discovers a clue, or realises what must be done to break the deadlock. Avoid situations where nothing happens, as a stalemate that simply stops the game is rarely interesting.
# **Momentum**

Remember that Characters can take Momentum from enemies in ways other than winning Opposed Melee Tests. Ranged attacks that inflict a Wound, for example, or anything that inflicts a Condition can also remove Momentum.
The GM needs to keep track of which NPCs and enemies have Momentum. You could mark an 'm' beside their Wounds, or place a counter next to their model to show when they have Momentum available.
# **THE GM'S TEST TOOLKIT**
There are several components of a Test, all of which are tools for the GM to use in fine-tuning the challenge presented to the Players.
#### **SL Modifiers**

These come from the Test's Difficulty and circumstances, or from a Character's Talents, equipment, and abilities. The GM determines the Difficulty, and may award up to +1 SL for a particularly clever approach. All SL Modifiers are applied after the dice are rolled.
#### **Advantage and Disadvantage**

This ability to reverse the numbers in your roll comes from Momentum (page 167), certain Talents, Spells, and Miracles, and from spending Fortune. The GM should almost never grant Advantage or inflict Disadvantage when the rules do not specifically call for it.
**Reroll:** A reroll is when you disregard the result of a dice roll, and roll it again. You must use the second result. Some Talents allow you to reroll, as does spending a point of Fortune.

**Rolling a Double:** Rolling a double means both the tens and the units die roll the same number (11, 22, 33, 44 and so on). This is most often relevant for triggering a Critical or Fumble in combat. It gives the GM the opportunity to introduce dramatic or amusing events for good or ill — feel free to get creative in describing what happens!
### **Extended Tests**

Extended Tests are used for lengthy or demanding tasks where time, resources, or repeated attempts matter, such as repairing armour or scouring the University of Altdorf 's library for mentions of exotic artefacts. If the exact time or cost isn't important, the GM can simply decide how long the task takes for someone with a relevant skill to perform.
Here's how it works:
boites: Opposed Tests
Something should always happen as a result of an Opposed
Test. Even when both Characters achieve the same SL and the
Test ends in a stalemate, use the result to point towards a way
forward. Perhaps neither side gains the upper hand, but one
notices a weakness, discovers a clue, or realises what must be
done to break the deadlock. Avoid situations where nothing
happens, as a stalemate that simply stops the game is rarely
interesting.
Momentum
Remember that Characters can take Momentum from enemies
in ways other than winning Opposed Melee Tests. Ranged
attacks that inflict a Wound, for example, or anything that
inflicts a Condition can also remove Momentum.
The GM needs to keep track of which NPCs and enemies have
Momentum. You could mark an ‘m’ beside their Wounds, or
place a counter next to their model to show when they have
Momentum available.
THE GM’S TEST TOOLKIT
There are several components of a Test, all of which are tools
for the GM to use in fine-tuning the challenge presented to the
Players.
SL Modifiers
These come from the Test’s Difficulty and circumstances, or
from a Character’s Talents, equipment, and abilities. The GM
determines the Difficulty, and may award up to +1 SL for a
particularly clever approach. All SL Modifiers are applied after
the dice are rolled.
Advantage and Disadvantage
This ability to reverse the numbers in your roll comes from
Momentum (page 167), certain Talents, Spells, and Miracles,
and from spending Fortune. The GM should almost never
grant Advantage or inflict Disadvantage when the rules do not
specifically call for it.
Reroll: A reroll is when you disregard the result of a dice roll, and
roll it again. You must use the second result. Some Talents allow
you to reroll, as does spending a point of Fortune.
Rolling a Double: Rolling a double means both the tens and the
units die roll the same number (11, 22, 33, 44 and so on). This
is most often relevant for triggering a Critical or Fumble in
combat. It gives the GM the opportunity to introduce dramatic
or amusing events for good or ill — feel free to get creative in
describing what happens!
Extended Tests
Extended Tests are used for lengthy or demanding tasks where
time, resources, or repeated attempts matter, such as repairing
armour or scouring the University of Altdorf ’s library for
mentions of exotic artefacts. If the exact time or cost isn’t
important, the GM can simply decide how long the task takes
for someone with a relevant skill to perform.
Here’s how it works:
Set the Goal: The GM sets the total SL required to succeed,
how often Tests can be made, any deadline, and what happens
if it is missed.
Choose the Test: The GM determines the Skill and Difficulty
or other SL modifiers for each attempt. This is usually the same
each time, but may change as the task progresses.
Track Progress: After each Test, add or subtract your SL from
the running total. A success always adds at least +1 SL, a failure
always subtracts at least -1 SL, a Critical adds at least +6 SL,
and a Fumble subtracts at least -6 SL.
You succeed when your total reaches the required SL. You fail if
your total ever drops below 0 SL, or if you run out of attempts
or time. The GM decides the consequences of failure and what,
if anything, was accomplished.
Characters can often work together on an Extended Test. Each
makes a Test and adds their SL to the shared total.
EXTEND CAUTION
Why are Extended Tests explained here rather than in the
Rules chapter? Because they are a tool for the GM to use
in particular circumstances. Overused, they can bog down
the game and feel anticlimactic. When a significant task
needs to feel exciting, a series of repeated dice rolls without
tension may fail to deliver.
Extended Tests work best for short, tense situations: you
have three Turns to pick this complicated lock before the
guard arrives — go! They can also show how much of a
larger task the Characters can complete before time runs
out, such as repairing a fortress before the orc horde arrives.
Avoid using them for adventure climaxes, or when a single
Test can resolve the situation just as well.

precedente: Elves can be encountered in the Empire, but are a rare sight
and very much hold themselves apart from other species. An
elf abroad in the Empire might be tasked with gathering
information for their homeland and attach themselves to a
band of adventurers to further this goal. Their long lives and
appreciation of art might see an elf spend years accompanying
an Artisan, Entertainer, or similar to witness their talent. They
may even align themselves with a band of scoundrels out of a
sense of adventure, or simple curiosity.
Knowing, vaguely, what sorts of adventures you intend to run
will help your players make useful choices — so it is a good
idea to let them in on a few details in advance, such as if their
Characters will be wandering about or staying in one general
area of the Old World for a time
Using The rUles
Most of what you need to know about the rules can be found in
Chapter 5, but there are a few that the GM needs to understand
in a slightly more in-depth way than players.
Fate and Fortune
Fortune can turn a disastrous situation in your Characters’
favour, so make spending it feel like a meaningful choice. When
a Character considers spending Fortune, ask whether they are
really sure they want to use it now, or whether they might need
it more later. Conversely, if they have Fortune left unused,
you can ask whether they want to spend it, implying that the
situation may be more dangerous than it first appears. These
moments should add drama to the decision without misleading
the players, making the choice to spend Fortune feel like a
moment of consequence rather than simply another resource.
Fate is another matter entirely. Spending Fate is a Big Deal: it is
powerful enough to cheat death. When a Character spends Fate
to survive, consider when they made the decision. If they spend
it before Damage is rolled (How Did That Miss?), their escape
can seem almost miraculously fortunate. They slip and the
decapitating strikes whistles harmlessly overhead or an arrow
rebounds off a Sigmarite medallion. If they use Fate after seeing
the result, in order to avoid death (Not Today!), make their
survival more desperate. Perhaps they are knocked unconscious
and only awaken after the battle, or are swept into fast-moving
water and carried a mile downstream before reaching the
bank. If they spend Fate to achieve the impossible (I Will Not
Fail!), describe how they tap into previously unknown reserves
of strength to hold the portcullis up long enough for their
companions to roll under, or how the grappling hook wedges
improbably in a crack of the wall, allowing them to climb up
just as the beastmen round the corner. Spending Fate should
always feel like a dramatic moment in the adventure.
Regaining Fate should be rare enough to feel momentous,
perhaps marking the culmination of a long campaign or the
achievement of an objective at considerable personal cost.
Fortune, by contrast, is replenished at the start of every session.
This assumes a session of around four hours. For longer sessions,
replenish Fortune at narratively appropriate moments, roughly
every four hours. For shorter sessions, replenish it every other
session to maintain a similar level of challenge.

md: # **The Reikland Diet**

The Reikland Diet is an assembly of the heads of the province's noble households that scrutinises and ratifies any decree made by the grand prince of the Reikland. The crown retains certain powers, however, including the right to summon and command the state army of the Reikland, the raising of emergency taxes in times of crisis, the right to authorise new coinage, and the right to call a High Lord Steward's Court should a powerful noble happen to face a criminal charge.

The diet meets as required in the Holzkrug Chamber of the Volkshalle in Altdorf, to either pass or return decrees to the crown with suggested amendments. As most lords of the Reikland Estates do not have time to attend the diet themselves, they generally send favoured children, spouses, relatives, or minions in their place. If an important decree is under scrutiny, worried lords from across the Reikland will attend in person.

This can be a source of friction, as several noble families of the Reikland have histories of feuding and one-upmanship. Nobles in the Empire guard their grievances as jealously as dwarfs, and there have been occasions when meetings at the Volkshalle have degenerated into belligerent barracking and even duelling.

Members of the diet are proud and do not like to feel that the grand prince is dictating the law without their due consideration. Until recently, Karl Franz had been an effective operator and the diet waved through most decrees without objection. Lately, the Emperor caused significant consternation when he issued a decree declaring Graf Sigismund von Jungfreud of Ubersreik to be a traitor. This declaration was announced after midnight to an almost empty chamber, thus securing support for Altdorf 's invasion of the Duchy of Ubersreik.
# **The Reikland Estates**

Vassals of the grand prince rule the Reikland Estates. They can do as they will with their lands, parcelling out fiefs to family and friends as they wish, though the creation of new hereditary titles requires the approval of the prince of Reikland and the Reikland Diet. Each estate has a range of distinct legal and military obligations to the crown, but all must build and maintain at least one regiment for the Reikland State Army,

> soldiers typically used in peacetime as watchmen, roadwardens, or guards. Most Reikland Estates are feudal, comprised of smaller fiefs ruled by vassals, many of whom hold hereditary titles that have existed for centuries.
#### **THE DUCHY OF WALLENSTEIN**

The Duchy of Wallenstein is the ancient demesne of the von Wallenstein family. It is a hilly region, sloping down from the rolling hills of the Hägercrybs to the sodden loam of the Teufel, Ober, and Tranig river valleys.

Graf Ferdinand von Wallenstein rules the duchy. He is a man of no obvious talent and a prodigious appetite for good cheer and ale. While he carouses in Nuln and Altdorf, his uncle, Lord Adelbert von Wallenstein, oversees the duchy from the family manor outside Auerswald. The Wallensteins come from an ancient line of proud warriors, dating back before the Age of Three Emperors. The Wallensteins have dynastic connections to several prominent Reikland families, not least House Holzkrug; the High Lord Ambassador is a relative and ally of the family.

Within the duchy lies the freistadt of Auerswald, whose charter from the emperor grants the town council authority over the town and its environs. The graf's lawyers, however, maintain that the rivers themselves lie beyond the freistadt's jurisdiction, allowing the noble rulers to levy taxes on all river traffic.

The duchy is wealthy, thanks to trade through Auerswald and the mineral riches beneath the Hägercrybs. Rumours across the Reikland claim the Hahnbrandt silver mine attracted the attention of the von Jungfreuds of Ubersreik, who maintain a claim to the duchy's southern and western territories. According to dramatic accusations in the Reikland Diet, these claims were merely a pretext for the Ubersreik graf's planned invasion of Wallenstein. There is little love lost between the von Jungfreuds and the von Wallensteins, whose feud stretches back centuries, but the only evidence presented by the Wallensteins amounts to hearsay and a purloined letter of dubious origin.

When Emperor Karl Franz declared Graf Sigismund von Jungfreud a traitor and sent several regiments from Altdorf to occupy Ubersreik, Graf Ferdinand and Lord Adelbert were careful to keep their opinions on the matter to themselves. Rumours cover the gamut of possibilities, some suggesting that Graf Ferdinand had a hand in the downfall of the Jungfreuds, while others suggest his dismay at Karl Franz's rash overreach is leading to a rapid reconciliation between the squabbling aristocrats.
#### **THE GRAF'S CHIEF VASSALS**

md: #### **Fencing**
Those with *Melee (Basic)* can use Fencing weapons, but cannot use their Weapon Qualities.
Unskilled Characters add the *Dangerous* Weapon Flaw.
# **Weapon Reach**
The lengths of the weapons are progressively bigger as follows.
- **Personal:** Your legs and fists, perhaps your head, and anything attached to those
- **Very Short:** Less than a foot in length
- **Short:** Up to 2 feet in length
- **Average:** Up to 3 feet long
- **Long:** Up to 6 foot long
- **Very Long:** Up to 10 feet in length; can Engage enemies up to 4 yards away, rather than just 2
- **Massive:** Anything over 10 feet long; can Engage enemies up to 6 yards away, rather than just 2
# **Weapon Reach and Defence**
If your weapon is longer than your opponent's, you benefit from +1 SL to defensive Melee Tests as you find it easier to keep them at bay.
# **HAND WEAPONS**
Hand Weapon is used to describe any of a number of basic weapons that, though different, are assumed to be effectively the same in-game, including axes, hammers, maces, short spears, and more.

Swords are a special hand weapon, being slightly deadlier than the other hand weapons and required skilled forging. They also bring a certain prestige to the wielder as they are the weapon of choice of the gentlefolk.

md: L'Épée de Khaine était effroyable à regarder et elle exerçait une influence imperceptible sur le Roi Phénix. Certains elfes, endurcis par les batailles, le rejoignirent dans un nouveau royaume, où les récits de leur cruauté valurent à sa cour une sombre réputation. Caledor, incapable de voir son vieil ami et seigneur lige sombrer dans la folie, le quitta et emmena les chevalier-dragons. En représailles, le Roi Phénix l'accusa de trahison et de division des forces des elfes.
**Le Grand Rituel**

Les démons du Chaos exploitèrent cette fracture et rassemblèrent la plus grande horde jamais vue pour attaquer Ulthuan. Tous les elfes, à l'exception d'Aenarion devenu fou, savaient qu'aucune armée ne pourrait la contrer et se désespérèrent d'avoir définitivement perdu la
guerre. La mort dans l'âme, Caledor décida seul de mettre en œuvre son plan et de faire venir les meilleurs sorciers d'Ulthuan sur l'Île des Morts, au centre de la Mer Intérieure.

Les légions démoniaques manœuvrèrent pour interrompre le rituel des elfes et Caledor lança un appel désespéré à Aenarion pour qu'il leur vienne en aide. Tout semblait perdu, mais au moment critique il arriva, repoussa l'attaque démoniaque et se sacrifia pour que le rituel puisse être achevé. Caledor, lui, abandonna son âme pour s'intégrer au vortex.

Ceci créa un vide magique soudain qui dévasta Ulthuan par des tempêtes et des tremblements de terre pendant trois jours. Quand le ciel s'éclaircit, les légions démoniaques, privées de magie brute, avaient disparu.
Les elfes entamèrent la reconstruction d'Ulthuan et désignèrent un nouveau Roi Phénix. Par la suite, ils prirent la mer pour explorer le monde et réparer l'ancien réseau de pierres gardiennes.

Pour renforcer le vortex de Caledor, les elfes commencèrent à lier leurs esprits à ces mégalithes, afin de continuer à participer au Grand Rituel par-delà la mort. Ils rencontrèrent de nouveau les nains, ce qui préfigurait une coopération entre les deux peuples.

Ils consolidèrent ensemble les lignes de force et améliorèrent la circulation de l'énergie magique vers le Vortex. Grâce à leurs efforts communs, la magie est drainée du monde aussi rapidement qu'elle y entre par les Portails du Warp.
# **DE L'HUILE SUR LE FEU**
# **La persécution des Sorciers avant Magnus**
*« Ne considérez pas les sorciers comme vos amis, car si leurs mots sont mielleux, le pouvoir qu'ils manipulent corrompt tout ce qu'il touche. Seule une flamme purificatrice peut y remédier. »*
— Dicta Sigmaris Divi (Altdorf, Ve siècle)

*« Ces imbéciles ne comprennent-ils pas que les merveilles qui résident dans l'Aethyr n'attendent que nous pour les plier à notre volonté ? Ils interdisent tout le bien que nous pourrions faire et nous menacent de châtiments comme si nous étions de mauvais garnements. Peu importe. Je ne peux pas oublier ce que j'ai vu et je m'y plongerai plus profondément, même si je risque la damnation. »*
— Journal de la baronne Magdalena Harrwitz von Kartwald, env. 1911 CI. Collection interdite du Temple de Sigmar.
# **Avant l'Empire et l'interdiction de Sigmar**

Une poignée d'humains a toujours été capable de percevoir et de manipuler les Vents de Magie, même si cela n'est pas courant. Leurs pouvoirs étaient utiles et faisaient des miracles inaccessibles pour les prêtres. Pourtant, le peuple et leurs chefs les craignaient : les sorciers perdaient trop souvent le contrôle de leur magie et subissaient d'horribles mutations, devenaient fous ou même périssaient. Certains étaient possédés par des démons ou servaient volontairement les Seigneurs du Chaos et attaquaient leurs semblables.
Ils étaient dangereux. Trop dangereux.

Sigmar lutta dans sa jeunesse contre les revenants impies du sorcier Nagash, menaçant d'envahir de Magie noire les terres qui deviendraient l'Empire. Il confia alors à son compagnon, Wolfgart Krieger, la défense de son royaume contre toutes les formes de magie. Les répurgateurs de l'Ordre du Marteau d'argent prétendent encore aujourd'hui que leur autorité provient de ce décret.

L'ascension de Sigmar et l'alliance avec les nains contre les gobelins conduisirent à l'unification des tribus humaines en une vaste fédération, l'Empire, mais également en un durcissement de l'opinion sur la sorcellerie. Selon une légende, les chefs des clans humains, menés par Sigmar, et ceux des nains sous l'égide du roi Kurgan Barbe-de-fer se réunirent massivement pour planifier la campagne qui finirait par la Bataille du Col du Feu noir. Cette assemblée fut interrompue par un groupe d'humains qui se faisait appeler les « Émissaires ».

Ils prétendaient étudier les constituants élémentaires du monde et affirmaient offrir leur sagesse et leurs pouvoirs contre les envahisseurs. Leurs vives démonstrations de loyauté influencèrent Sigmar, même si le roi Kurgan lui déconseilla d'avoir confiance en une quelconque magie, à l'exception de celle des dieux et des ancêtres. La raison de l'alliance ne tenait qu'à un fil et ils avaient besoin d'aide. Sigmar accepta leur offre, mais il faillit mourir dans leur piège.

À la lueur du feu du conseil, les sorciers se révélèrent alliés des gobelins, déchaînant leurs sorts et invoquant des démons. Face à cette horde, Sigmar manqua de tomber, mais il fut sauvé de justesse par le marteau de Kurgan. Finalement victorieux, il examina les décombres, les camarades blessés et les morts, et réalisa sa folie.

Après avoir défait les peaux-vertes, le moment était venu pour Sigmar de fonder l'Empire et de s'autoproclamer Empereur. Peu après, il semblerait même le jour de son couronnement, il décréta l'interdiction de toute sorcellerie dans l'Empire, sous peine de mort.
À son ascension, cette loi devint l'ordre d'un dieu.
# **La persécution**

Dans les premiers temps, les Comtes Électeurs firent rigoureusement appliquer le commandement de Sigmar. De nombreux cultes les soutenaient activement, particulièrement ceux de Verena et de Morr, qui désiraient éradiquer les ennemis cachés et éliminer les blasphémateurs… et les éventuels concurrents. À mesure que le Culte de Sigmar prenait de l'ampleur, ses fidèles les plus dévoués se montrèrent les plus doués pour débusquer les sorciers introuvables.

Le Grand Rituel
Les démons du Chaos exploitèrent cette fracture et
rassemblèrent la plus grande horde jamais vue pour attaquer

fou, savaient qu’aucune armée ne pourrait la contrer et se
désespérèrent d’avoir définitivement perdu la
guerre. La mort dans l’âme, Caledor décida
seul de mettre en œuvre son plan et
de faire venir les meilleurs sorciers
d’Ulthuan sur l’Île des Morts, au
centre de la Mer Intérieure.

manœuvrèrent pour interrompre

*Vous empêchez que la civilisation soit envahie par la vermine à l'aide de vos fidèles compagnons canins.*

Les Ratiers patrouillent dans toutes les villes et les cités, et ce, pour une bonne raison. Les rues de l'Empire débordent de déchets puants de nourritures diverses, le parfait terreau pour la prolifération de la vermine. Les Ratiers gagnent leur croûte en tuant ces rats, en nettoyant les caves de leurs nids et en plongeant au cœur des égouts de l'Empire, qui en sont littéralement infestés… à condition qu'ils soient assez courageux pour affronter les autres créatures qui y pullulent. Au début de leur formation, la plupart des Ratiers adoptent un chiot qu'ils entraînent à la chasse aux rats. Les Ratiers sont engagés par les villes et deviennent des Égoutiers qui partent à la chasse aux rats géants et autres nuisances souterraines. Il arrive quelquefois que des villes entières soient envahies par les rats, auquel cas elles font appel à des Exterminateurs.
*« Tu vois là au milieu de la pile, Otmar ? Il y en a un gros ! Fais gaffe qu'il soit bien mort avant de le choper. Sinon, il te mordra la main avec ses dents empoisonnées. »*
– Annaliese Rattenfänger, Égoutière
*« Désolé, mon ami. C'est le reste de la guilde qui s'occupe des rats. Mes amis et moi, on s'occupe des trucs plus gros dans les égouts. Il y en a des flopées, en dessous… »*
– Mårten Stormdal, Exterminateur d'Ubersreik

Les Ratiers changent de ville lorsque les rats deviennent « trop gros » ou « trop intelligents », ou encore lorsque la compétition est trop féroce. Lorsqu'ils voyagent, ils peuvent se lier d'amitié avec ceux qui acceptent l'aide d'un frondeur des rues, d'autant que les ratiers sont partants pour s'aventurer là ou d'autres refusent de se rendre.

Si vous voulez jouer un Personnage qui sait ce que sont ces « trop gros » ou « trop intelligents » skavens (voir page 336), le Ratier est fait pour vous. Cependant, les skavens ont pour habitude d'assassiner ceux qui lancent des rumeurs à leur sujet. De ce fait, les Ratiers les plus sages ne partageront généralement pas ce qu'ils savent, certains allant même jusqu'à s'appuyer sur leur expérience professionnelle pour discréditer ces histoires de « grands rats » ou « hommes-rats ».

precedente: MILICIEN
Halfling, Haut Elfe, Humain, Nain
Vous êtes les garants de la paix et vous maintenez l’ordre parmi la
populace pour que votre ville ne sombre pas dans l’anarchie.
Les Miliciens sont employés par les autorités locales afin de
patrouiller les rues de l’Empire. La plupart ne sont autres que des
gardiens de la paix engagés volontaires et bien peu connaissent
les lois qu’ils sont censés faire appliquer. La corruption est
endémique, et de nombreux Miliciens s’engagent auprès des
autorités dans le seul but de blesser les autres ou encore de
venir en aide aux gangs de criminels du coin. Certains arrivent
à tripler leurs soldes en fermant ainsi les yeux.
Seules quelques villes et cités disposent de Miliciens
professionnels qui sont payés pour comprendre et faire
respecter les lois. Dans de nombreux cas, la Paix de l’Empereur
est maintenue par l’Armée, dont les hommes surveillent les
remparts, les portes et effectuent des patrouilles dans les rues
en respectant les consignes de leurs supérieurs.
« Je suis donc allée jusqu’à Middenheim, le pays d’Ulrich, et qu’est-ce
que j’y ai vu ? Je te jure, plus de la moitié de leur Milice est composée
de femmes ! J’y serai restée jusqu’à la fin de ma carrière si j’avais
pu. »
– Jana Tennisohn,
Inspectrice en chef (à la retraite) Milicien de Nuln
«  Je suis désolé, monsieur, j’ai un assassin halfling, un réseau de
contrebande de mystracine, une guerre de gang et un noble qui
menace de me faire arrêter par ma propre Milice. Votre chat disparu
devra attendre jusqu’à demain. »
– Sergent Harri Makkenpieser, Milicien d’Altdorf
Tous les Miliciens ne sont pas malhonnêtes, mais ceux qui ont
une certaine éthique sont très vite désabusés par la corruption
qui pollue le système. En rejoignant des groupes d’aventuriers,
ces Miliciens peuvent défendre la justice selon leurs propres
termes. L’expérience de la rue fait d’eux des combattants d’une
grande efficacité au sein d’un petit groupe, et leur présence
dans ledit groupe peut aider à donner une légitimité à cette
bande de bons à rien.

md: La monotonie du voyage représente pour de nombreux Personnages le moment idéal pour pratiquer leurs Compétences en vue des épreuves à venir. Un Personnage peut effectuer un Test **Intermédiaire (+0)** d'une seule Compétence qu'il est possible de pratiquer en voyageant : Orientation, Métier (Herboristerie), Langue (Wastelander), etc. Une Réussite signifie que le Personnage peut inverser le résultat d'un Test en utilisant cette Compétence au cours de l'aventure suivante, ou de toute étape ultérieure du voyage.
### **Récupérer**

Les voyages sont généralement peu propices au repos : marcher à travers les forêts et sur des chemins de montagne, dormir à la belle étoile dans un froid mordant ou une chaleur brûlante, se cacher des monstres et autres terribles menaces. Ce ne sont pas des situations souvent conseillées par les médecins traitants. Mais vous avez fait des efforts particuliers pour ne pas vous surmener. Vous pouvez comptabiliser cette Étape comme s'il s'agissait d'un « repos » dans le cadre de la guérison des Blessures, conformément à la page 181 du **Livre de Règles**. Vous ne pouvez pas choisir cette Activité si, pour une raison quelconque, vous avez souffert d'un État *Exténué* pendant cette Étape du voyage.
#### **Monter un camp**

Souvent, les voyageurs se concentrent trop sur la destination et pas assez sur le voyage lui-même ; à l'arrivée, ils sont hagards, épuisés et mal préparés à ce qu'ils vont affronter. N'importe qui peut planter une tente ou déployer une couverture. Les voyageurs chevronnés, eux, prennent le temps de s'installer confortablement pour la nuit en choisissant un bon emplacement, en ramassant du bois de chauffage, en préparant de l'eau, etc. Effectuez un Test de **Survie en extérieur** ou de **Guérison Intermédiaire (+0)**. Chaque DR de l'un ou l'autre de ces Tests peut être dépensé pour retirer les État *Exténué* d'un Personnage ou pour le guérir (voir page 123 du **Livre de Règles**).
### **RENCONTRES**

Voyager dans le Vieux Monde est tout sauf prévisible. Patrouilleurs routiers paranoïaques, marchands intrépides et pèlerins consciencieux se pressent sur les grand-routes de l'Empire, tandis que les sentiers moins empruntés abritent des bandes de mutants, des péages illégaux et des bandits à l'affût. Les Personnages peuvent faire l'expérience de tels événements au hasard ou non, mais toutes les Rencontres doivent ajouter à la saveur du voyage, ou aux thèmes et à la narration de l'histoire en cours.
### RENCONTRES POSITIVES

Les Rencontres positives sont généralement bénéfiques, bien que de nombreux groupes trouvent toujours le moyen de retourner une situation contre eux ! Les Rencontres positives peuvent être déclenchées par un Succès Impressionnant ou mieux, lors d'un voyage ou simplement si vous souhaitez récompenser les Personnages pour avoir été particulièrement intelligents ou bien préparés.

# **Clanrat**

Most skaven are clanrats, hailing from one of the many complex skaven clans that constantly bicker, politic, backstab, and eventually war on each other. They generally act on the orders of higher-status skaven, but are always looking for a way to secure a better position, most often by betrayal. They usually dress in mouldering leather or filthy cloth, with scraps of rusty and tarnished metal serving as makeshift armour. Clanrats are often sent out as scouts or raiders to scavenge for goods, search for warpstone, or raid for slaves.

THE LOATHSOME RATMEN
Skaven are a malevolent species of ratmen eking out a foul
existence in the sewers and tunnels beneath the Empire’s cities,
watching, waiting, and plotting. So rarely are they seen that
those who do glimpse them usually dismiss them as beastmen
or mutants. Few suspect the truth: an Under-Empire stretches
beneath the Old World, its tunnels linking every major city
and beyond.
Skaven society is built upon the labour of captives taken
from across the Old World, and their network of spies and
informants is vast. The unscrupulous supply prisoners and
warpstone to the skaven in exchange for secret knowledge and
other unsavoury favours.
The skaven know their survival depends upon secrecy and
protect it ruthlessly. Those foolish enough to speak openly of a
civilisation of intelligent ratmen beneath the Empire’s cobbled
streets may soon be found dead in a gutter, the unfortunate
victim of an unlikely accident.
‘I never seen nothin’. There were no
ratmen, you hear? Just bad luck. Wilbur
slipped and fell, that’s all. He got
careless, fell down a ladder onto his own
knife. Ten times. Just bad luck.’
— Kristiana Fellger, retired Sewer Jack
